attempts.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of electrodialysis (ED) and its variants, from principles and device operation to performance, applications, and current challenges.

What electrodialysis is and how it works
- ED uses an electric potential applied across alternating cation- and anion-exchange membranes to drive ion transport and split a feed stream into a diluted (low-salinity) and a concentrated (high-salinity) effluent. <cite id="25b06b50-0">The principle of Electrodialysis relies on the selective permeability of ion exchange membranes to cations and anions; upon entering the ED stack, feed ions migrate through membranes under applied potential, with hydroxide generation at cathodes and acidification at anodes, while the diluate is demineralized and the concentrate is enriched</cite> <cite id="de245b43-0">In ED desalination, chambers separated by ion-selective membranes transport negative ions through anion-permeable layers and positive ions through cation-permeable layers toward oppositely charged electrodes, concentrating ions in some chambers and leaving desalinated water in others</cite>.
- Core transport mechanisms include migration and diffusion under electric driving force, coupled with electroosmotic water transport; at higher voltages, both ion migration and associated water drag increase. <cite id="25b06b50-1">Water migration in ED primarily occurs via electroosmotic drag accompanying ion transport, and increasing voltage enhances both ion migration rates and associated water movement</cite>.
- Operation is governed by mass-transport and charge balance. Limiting current density (LCD) marks the onset of boundary-layer depletion (concentration polarization), raising resistance, lowering salt rejection and current efficiency; operation above LCD triggers water splitting to sustain current (overlimiting regime) at the expense of efficiency. <cite id="25b06b50-2">When operating current density approaches or exceeds the critical LCD, concentration polarization causes depletion of counter-ions at the diluate-side membrane surface and accumulation of co-ions at the concentrate-side surface, increasing membrane resistance, decreasing salt rejection, and decreasing current efficiency</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-3">LCD is a core design parameter; experimentally determined LCDs derive from boundary-layer thickness and are proportional to ion concentration and diffusivity, with polarization-induced depletion at the diluate interface and co-ion accumulation at the concentrate interface; further increasing current density above threshold dissociates water at the boundary layer (water splitting), increasing total current and decreasing current efficiency</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-4">Limiting transport numbers of counterions define LCDs for cation/anion membranes; the system LCD is the minimum absolute value across membrane types, ensuring operation below threshold to avoid excessive depletion or polarization</cite>.

Device components and modes
- A typical ED stack comprises alternating cation- and anion-exchange membranes; ED can be operated in selective demineralization, concentration, or conversion modes, with ED reversal (EDR) swapping selective cation/anion transport per compartment to enhance acid/base production from salts. <cite id="de245b43-0">An ED membrane stack comprises alternately placed cation- and anion-exchange membranes; the process can demineralize, concentrate, and/or convert salt-containing solutions</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-1">Stack voltage/current density trade-offs govern ion concentration, energy consumption, and water migration; e.g., 60 V optimized Li+ concentration while moderating energy loss and co-ion migration</cite>.
- Bipolar membranes enable electrochemically assisted transport and in situ acid–base generation; ED with bipolar membranes (BMED) is widely used to produce organic and inorganic acids/bases from salts. <cite id="7ee2a26c-0">ED with bipolar membranes (BMED) dissociates water into H+ and OH− across the bipolar layer, yielding acidic and alkaline currents and enabling production and purification of acids (e.g., propionic, gluconic, salicylic) and bases from corresponding salts</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Bipolar electrodialysis concentrates and purifies acids/bases; compared to conventional ED, it produces 51-fold (HCl) and 63-fold (H2SO4) acid concentration and nine-fold NaOH base concentration with minimal co-contaminant carryover</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-3">EDB systems integrate anionic, cationic, and bipolar membranes to generate acid and base; such systems have long industrial use (e.g., seawater desalination to acid/base products) and are increasingly applied to wastewater treatment and food/biochemical processing</cite>.
- ED can be coupled to ion-exchange columns to form electrodeionization (EDI), integrating electrostatic regeneration to sustain high-resistivity product water. <cite id="7ee2a26c-2">ED variants include conventional ED, electro-electrodialysis (EED), BMED, and electrodialysis deionization (EDI), with ED widely used for separation and production and increasingly for resource recovery from wastewaters and brines</cite>.

Performance metrics and operating regimes
- Energy consumption depends on salinity, conductivity, membrane properties, and system design. Reported specific energy consumption (SEC) spans roughly 2.2–6.6 kWh/m3 across studies and configurations. <cite id="de245b43-0">Specific energy consumption for seawater desalination has been reduced from 6.6 to 3.6 kWh/m3; optimized multistage configurations for artificial waters at 510 nM reach 2.2 kWh/m3, close to RO values of 1.8 kWh/m3; seawater multistage achieved 3 kWh/m3; temperature increases reduce electrical resistance by ~2% per °C, lowering energy</cite> <cite id="de245b43-1">A multistage ED configuration achieved 3.6 kWh/m3 to desalinate from 500 mM to 200 mM, requiring at least four stages to reach drinking-quality synthetic seawater, and consumed twice the energy of state-of-the-art RO in a non-optimized system</cite> <cite id="de245b43-3">Hybrid RO–ED systems can approach SEC thresholds as low as 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 for seawater when integrated with salinity-gradient processes (FO, PRO, RED), with ED contributing electricity-driven desalination at 2–6 kWh/m3</cite>.
- Salt rejection and selectivity depend on membrane charge, ion valence, and current density. <cite id="de245b43-0">Advances in multivalent-selective membranes enable elimination of multivalent cations (e.g., Mg2+, Ca2+), reducing scaling risk and improving selective demineralization</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-0">BME systems have been used to produce and purify acids (e.g., gluconic, salicylic), with BM dissociating water to transport protons and hydroxide ions through the membrane layers, enabling acid–base separation</cite>.
- Current efficiency and polarization control: <cite id="25b06b50-2">Approaching or exceeding LCD induces concentration polarization with high resistance, lower salt rejection, and reduced current efficiency; thus, current density must be controlled to avoid depletion of counter-ions at the diluate interface</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-3">LCD determines boundary-layer transport and mass-transport-limited operation; beyond threshold, water splitting raises current and reduces efficiency</cite>.
- Temperature affects ionic mobility, boundary-layer transport, and membrane properties. <cite id="995d701f-2">Between 25 and 50 °C, SEC decreased 28%; between 50–75 °C, a modest 1.5% decrease was observed (possible due to non-linear conductivity and component resistivity changes); between 75–85 °C, SEC fell 23% with a 41% current-efficiency increase, though higher temperatures may increase co-ion transport and purity risks, warranting further study</cite>.

Module and process innovations
- Pulsed electric-field ED (PEF-ED) can lower SEC and mitigate polarization by introducing relaxation phases. <cite id="995d701f-3">Shifting from continuous to pulsed electric field in ED generally decreases SEC, especially at high current densities where polarization is severe; optimal pulse frequency thresholds lie around 0.02–0.05 Hz depending on operating current; reducing duty cycle yields moderate energy savings, while increasing duty reduces operating time; applying current during relaxation periods further reduces SEC without compromising throughput and attenuates concentration polarization</cite>.
- Staging and staged operation tailor the driving force and residence time per compartment to approach RO-like energy at optimized conditions. <cite id="de245b43-1">Multistage ED matched single-stage performance for 200–500 mM desalination but required at least four stages to reach 3.6 kWh/m3 for synthetic seawater, demonstrating that staging adapts driving force to stage-specific conditions at lower energy</cite>.
- Flow design and inter-electrode spacing influence water drag and ion/cosolute transport. <cite id="25b06b50-1">Increasing voltage increases ion migration and electroosmotic water movement; stack voltage and flow conditions were optimized to maximize Li+ concentration while limiting energy loss and undesired water co-migration</cite>.
- Integration with filtration and other separations: <cite id="995d701f-0">Recent electrodialytic developments include electroconvective vortices, pulsed electric fields, electrodeionization, and shock electrodialysis; ED combined with filtration membranes (EDFM) is proposed for eco-efficient circular-economy strategies</cite>.
- Thermal management and antiscalant strategies: <cite id="de245b43-0">Temperature increases reduce electrical resistance by ~2% per °C, lowering ED energy consumption; ED is compatible with renewable energy and small-scale deployment</cite> <cite id="995d701f-2">At 85 °C, SEC decreased 23% and current efficiency rose 41%, though co-ion transport increased, suggesting a trade-off between energy, selectivity, and membrane stability that requires careful optimization</cite>.

Variants and hybrid systems
- Electrodeionization (EDI): combines ED with ion-exchange to continuously regenerate resins and produce high-purity water; EDI modules are widely deployed for demineralization and are part of the broader ED family. <cite id="7ee2a26c-2">Electrodialysis deionization (EDI) integrates with CED/EED/BMED to achieve high-resistivity product water via electrostatic ion removal and in situ regeneration</cite>.
- Bipolar electrodialysis (BMED) and reverse electrodialysis (RED): BMED produces acids/bases from salts; RED harvests energy from salinity gradients and can be integrated with RO to reduce net energy. <cite id="7ee2a26c-0">BMED dissociates water across bipolar membranes to generate acid and base currents, enabling acid/base recovery and purification from salts</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Bipolar ED concentrated acids up to 51× (HCl) and 63× (H2SO4) and produced 9× concentrated NaOH with low impurity levels relative to feed</cite> <cite id="de245b43-3">Hybrid RO–RED/FO/PRO systems can approach 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 for seawater desalination by leveraging salinity-gradient energy, with ED/RED contributing electricity-driven separations in the 2–6 kWh/m3 range</cite>.
- Selective ED and fractionation: using monovalent-selective membranes enables fractionation of ions by valence (e.g., Li+/Mg2+), supporting downstream recovery of valuable metals and acids. <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Selective electrodialysis (SED) replaces standard CEM/AEM with monovalent-selective membranes to fractionate monovalent and divalent ions (e.g., Li+ vs. Mg2+), enabling separation of inorganic acids and metal ions and facilitating recovery from process streams</cite>.

Applications
- Desalination and brine management: <cite id="de245b43-0">ED has industrial heritage in seawater and brackish desalination; while advances in RO have reduced new ED plant deployment for seawater, ED remains competitive for certain waters (≈2.2–3.6 kWh/m3) and is easily renewable-powered</cite> <cite id="de245b43-1">For synthetic seawater, ED multistage achieved 3.6 kWh/m3 to 200 mM, but non-optimized setups can be double RO’s energy; staging mitigates driving-force losses</cite>.
- Environmental treatment and circular economy: <cite id="995d701f-0">Electrodialytic processes are promising for wastewater treatment, food preservation, bioactive compound production, organic acid extraction, and energy recovery, with emerging techniques (pulsed fields, electroconvective vortices, electrodeionization, shock ED) boosting interest</cite> <cite id="995d701f-4">ED is considered an advanced treatment for removing organic ions at ambient temperature/pressure without harmful chemicals, with demonstrated roles in minimal liquid discharge (MLD) and zero-liquid discharge (ZLD) systems to minimize brine discharge and recover water, minerals, salts, and metals</cite>.
- Industrial acid/base and nutrient recovery: <cite id="7ee2a26c-0">BMED has produced organic acids (e.g., salicylic acid) and is effective in wastewater treatment by generating acid/base streams in situ without waste streams</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Acid/base recovery via bipolar ED achieved high concentration factors with low impurity carryover, enabling resource value recovery from industrial effluents</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-2">ED processes are increasingly applied to recover nitrogen, phosphorus, precious metals, and organic compounds from byproducts, wastewaters, and brines</cite>.
- Battery material production and specialty separations: <cite id="995d701f-2">In membrane electrodialysis for lithium hydroxide (LiOH) production, SEC decreased 28% from 25–50 °C, ~1.5% from 50–75 °C, and 23% from 75–85 °C, with current efficiency 41% higher at 85 °C; temperature increases improved ionic mobility and boundary-layer diffusion but increased co-ion transport risks</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-0">Voltage/current density tuning governs ion removal and water quality; for Li+ concentration, 60 V maximized Li+ to 18.12 g/L while balancing energy loss and water migration</cite>.
- Pharmaceutical and toxic compound removal: <cite id="995d701f-4">ED has been used for removal of harmful metallic ions and organic ions such as 4-nitrophenol with high removal efficiency, compact installations, and short treatment times, operating without harmful reagents</cite>.

Limitations, challenges, and mitigation
- Concentrate polarization, co-ion permeation, and scaling: <cite id="25b06b50-2">Operation near or above LCD induces polarization with surface ion depletion/recovery cycles that raise resistance, reduce salt rejection, and lower current efficiency</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-3">Above LCD, water splitting at boundary layers increases total current while decreasing current efficiency due to hydroxide/oxide formation and added transport needs</cite>.
- Fouling and antiscalants: <cite id="995d701f-4">ED is compatible with ambient conditions and avoids chemical additives in many separations, but high salinity and hardness in brines elevate scaling risk; ED is often integrated in MLD/ZLD to manage brines and recover resources, yet must address energy and scaling challenges</cite>.
- Scale-up and real-life constraints: <cite id="995d701f-0">Despite promising new membrane phenomena (electroconvective vortices, pulsed fields, electrodeionization, shock ED) and market evolution, hurdles remain in scale-up and real-life conditions; integration into circular-economy strategies is growing but deployment challenges persist</cite>.
- Energy and selectivity trade-offs: <cite id="de245b43-1">Even optimized ED can exceed RO energy by twofold without deeper process intensification, highlighting the need for improved stack/module hydrodynamics, staging, and membrane selectivity</cite> <cite id="995d701f-2">Higher temperatures can cut SEC and improve current efficiency but may increase co-ion transport and purity risks, requiring membrane and operating point trade-offs</cite>.
- Emerging mitigation strategies: <cite id="995d701f-3">Pulsed electric-field ED reduces SEC by attenuating polarization and using relaxation cycles; tailored pulse frequency (~0.02–0.05 Hz) and duty cycles provide significant energy savings with minimal throughput loss, and applying low current during relaxation helps attenuate polarization while maintaining transport</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-0">Voltage/current-density control balances ion removal and energy loss; excess voltage increases both ion and water transport, risking unwanted dilute-side co-ion migration</cite>.
- Materials and membranes: <cite id="25b06b50-2">Recent anion-exchange membrane advances showed higher limiting current densities and better electrodialysis performance than commercial AEMs, enabling higher current densities with low area resistance and improved stability</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-2">Ion-exchange membrane research targets improved selectivity, stability, and resource recovery from complex wastewaters and brines within the broader ED family</cite>.

Practical takeaways and outlook
- ED is a versatile electro-membrane process for desalination, ion concentration, and electrochemical conversion, with demonstrated energy ranges from ~2.2 to 6.6 kWh/m3 depending on water type and system configuration, and compatibility with renewable energy and small modular deployments. <cite id="de245b43-0">Specific energy consumption spans 2.2–6.6 kWh/m3 across optimized and seawater conditions; ED is easy to couple to renewable electricity and suitable for small-scale and mobile systems</cite>.
- Advances in pulsed-field operation, staging, selective membranes (including monovalent-selective and multivalent rejection), and ED-RO hybrids are narrowing energy gaps and expanding applicability to circular-economy goals, wastewater treatment, and specialty separations. <cite id="995d701f-3">Pulsed electric-field ED can reduce energy via polarization mitigation and optimized pulse/duty parameters</cite> <cite id="de245b43-1">Staged ED adapts driving force and residence time to approach lower energy targets</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Selective ED and BMED enable ion and acid/base fractionation and high-concentration recovery from industrial streams</cite> <cite id="de245b43-3">ED/RED-RO hybrids can push net SEC toward 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 by harvesting salinity-gradient energy</cite>.
- Key challenges remain in large-scale robustness, polarization/scaling control, and maintaining selectivity–energy trade-offs; continued progress in membrane materials, module hydrodynamics, and process integration is central to broader industrialization and ZLD/MLD deployments. <cite id="995d701f-0">Scale-up and real-life hurdles are significant despite promising new membrane phenomena and market development; integration into circular-economy strategies is accelerating but constrained by deployment issues</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-2">Limiting current and polarization management are essential to sustain salt rejection and current efficiency</cite>.

Notes on related electromembrane processes
- Electromembrane processes share the core physics of ion transport through charged membranes under electric fields and include ED, EDR, BMED, EDI, MCDI, and RED. <cite id="7ee2a26c-4">Electromembrane processes—ED, EDR (reversal), BMED, EDI, MCDI, and RED—share ion migration across charged membranes; reviews discuss scaling mitigation, mass-transfer enhancement, and hybrid process development, with critical analyses of RED-based energy production</cite>.
- Coupling ED with reverse osmosis, forward osmosis, or pressure-retarded osmosis is an active area to leverage hydraulic and electrochemical gradients for lower net energy and higher water recovery in brine management. <cite id="de245b43-3">Hybrids of RO with FO, RED, or PRO can approach SEC of 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 for seawater by harnessing salinity-gradient energy, with ED/RED modules providing electricity-driven separations in 2–6 kWh/m3 ranges</cite>.

Title: Trade-Off between Operating Time and Energy Consumption in Pulsed Electric Field Electrodialysis: A Comprehensive Simulation Study
Snippet: In this work, the effect of the input signal parameters on the performance of pulsed electric field electrodialysis has been systematically evaluated using a facile simulation model solved applying finite element methods. Different parameters, such as pulse frequency, duty cycle or applied current density in both the pulse and relaxation phases have been evaluated in terms of the specific energy consumption and operating time needed to achieve a constant transport of charges through the membranes. In general, it can be concluded that changing from continuous to PEF modes implies a general decrease in specific energy consumption; being this improvement more significant at high current densities, where high degrees of polarization are reached. There is a threshold frequency value from which further improvements in energy consumption become almost negligible. This frequency depends on the level of applied current i high , taking a value of 0.02 Hz for 0.7·i lim and increasing up to 0.05 Hz for 1.2·i lim . Decreasing the duty cycle provides moderate savings in energy consumption, while increasing it implies significant reductions in the operating time needed for a given desalination process. For the first time, a novel type of PEF function with application of current during the relaxation periods has been evaluated. These new PEF modes are found to be a promising strategy to effectively reduce the specific energy consumption, without compromising the operating time of ED processes. Application of low levels of current density during the relaxation periods is useful for attenuating concentration polarization, while maintaining ion transport during the entire ED operating time.
</snippet>

Title: Electrodialysis as a potential technology for 4-nitrophenol abatement from wastewater
Snippet: For several decades, electrodialysis (ED) has been widely used for the isolation of chemical compounds dissolved in water, such as water desalination, acid concentrations, mineral recovery, and removal of harmful metallic ions (Danaeifar et al. 2023;Li et al. 2023;Lotfy et al. 2022;Martí-Calatayud et al. 2012;Pramanik et al. 2017;Tian et al. 2021), among others. In these processes, its relevance is attributed to both its removal efficiency and its main operative advantages, including compact installations and short treatment times (Chang et al. 2010;Lotfy et al. 2022). In environmental terms, it is considered advanced, since it allows the removal of organic ions by innocuous processes, carried out at room temperature and pressure and without the addition of harmful chemical compounds (Bernardes et al. 2014;Rajoria et al. 2022). 

About a new promising application, the ED can be included as a technological step in novel integral processes known as minimal (MLD) or zero liquid discharge (ZLD), whose main purpose is the pollution control for environmental and human health protection (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2023). These systems address the elimination or minimization the brine discharge, from natural and industrial brine effluents, and recover valuable resources such as water, minerals, salts, and metals, among others. Technologies such as reverse osmosis (RO), forward osmosis (FO), brine concentrator (BC), and brine crystallizer (BCr), among others, also can be considered in these processes (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2022a). However, this must still overcome several drawbacks associated with the high energy consumption, emerging scale, and employment of fossil fuels as energy sources, among others (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2022b). In this context, the ED is an adequate choice to contemplate in these systems since it has been used industrially on a large scale for several decades.

Snippet: Electrodialysis (ED) is an electro-membrane ion separation process widely used to demineralize, concentrate, and/or convert salt-containing solutions [1][2][3][4]. Moreover, ED appears as an emerging technology for nutrient recovery in wastewater treatment [5][6][7][8]. The driving force for the salt separation is the application of an electrical potential across an ED membrane stack, whereby charged particles are removed from the feed solution. An ED membrane stack comprises alternately placed cation-and anion-exchange membranes. During ED, the feed stream is separated into two streams, one with a reduced concentration of ions (diluate), and the other enriched with ions (concentrate). From the techno-economical point of view, it is important to run ED under optimal operating conditions [9][10][11][12]. Various parameters, such as feed solution composition, temperature, flow, membrane characteristics, spacers, applied power, and current density, impact the ED process efficiency [2,[13][14][15][16][17][18]. One of the core parameters for the ED process design is the limiting current density (LCD) [19][20][21][22][23]. The experimentally determined LCD is commonly used for deriving the process essential boundary layer thickness, and it is directly proportional to the ion concentration and diffusivity [20,22,24]. The boundary layer is a thin layer of the solution adjacent to the membrane surface, with a concentration decrease of counter-ions on the diluate side and a concentration increase of co-ions on the concentrate side, compared to the bulk concentration [16]. The LCD indicates the electric current density that leads to the depletion of ions in the boundary layer on the diluate side, as a result of the concentration polarization [24]. With a further increase of the current density above a certain threshold, a dissociation of water molecules to H + and OH − ions occurs in the boundary layer as an undesired effect, causing an increase of the overall current density and subsequently a decrease in the current efficiency.
</snippet>

Snippet: Abstract Electrodialysis (ED) is currently used for selective removal of ions and brackish water desalination, while for seawater desalination ED is considered to be too energy intensive. This research focuses on the viability of ED using multiple stages for seawater desalination. With staging, the driving force is adapted to the governing conditions at that specific stage, operating at its individual optimum at lower energy consumption. An ED multistage configuration is examined that contains up to four stages. We compare single stage with multistage ED and investigate the effect of operation parameters. Different current densities are applied and optimized and residence time is compared to describe both transmembrane salt and water fluxes. We showed that desalination from 500 mM to 200 mM is possible, but that for these desalination conditions a multistage and single-stage system perform equal. Operation of each stage of the multistage close to limiting current density shows that desalination of synthetic seawater close to drinking water quality is possible. Title: Innovations in electromembrane processes
Snippet: Electromembrane processes are increasingly important group of separation methods, widely used for removal of charged components from solutions. It is a growing field of research with a plethora of both existing and still developed applications. The separation is based on ion migration across the charged membranes (a polymeric matrix with fixed charged groups, counterbalanced with mobile counter-ions), placed in the electric field. This paper presents the main electromembrane processes: electrodialysis (ED), electrodialysis reversal (EDR), electrodialysis with bipolar membrane (EDBM), electrodeionization (EDI), membrane capacitive deionization (MCDI), reverse electrodialysis (RED). We present the common applications of electromembrane processes and discuss the physical basis of the electromembrane processes. The most important parameters of the ion-exchange membranes are discussed, as well as the novel approaches towards mitigation of scaling, enhancement of mass transfer, decreasing the concentration polarization, and new hybrid electromembrane processes. Critical analysis of the possibility of energy production by reverse electrodialysis is presented.

Reported specific energy consumption (SEC) spans roughly 2.2–6.6 kWh/m3 across studies and configurations. <cite id="de245b43-0">Specific energy consumption for seawater desalination has been reduced from 6.6 to 3.6 kWh/m3; optimized multistage configurations for artificial waters at 510 nM reach 2.2 kWh/m3, close to RO values of 1.8 kWh/m3; seawater multistage achieved 3 kWh/m3; temperature increases reduce electrical resistance by ~2% per °C, lowering energy</cite> <cite id="de245b43-1">A multistage ED configuration achieved 3.6 kWh/m3 to desalinate from 500 mM to 200 mM, requiring at least four stages to reach drinking-quality synthetic seawater, and consumed twice the energy of state-of-the-art RO in a non-optimized system</cite> <cite id="de245b43-3">Hybrid RO–ED systems can approach SEC thresholds as low as 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 for seawater when integrated with salinity-gradient processes (FO, PRO, RED), with ED contributing electricity-driven desalination at 2–6 kWh/m3</cite>.
- Salt rejection and selectivity depend on membrane charge, ion valence, and current density. <cite id="de245b43-0">Advances in multivalent-selective membranes enable elimination of multivalent cations (e.g., Mg2+, Ca2+), reducing scaling risk and improving selective demineralization</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-0">BME systems have been used to produce and purify acids (e.g., gluconic, salicylic), with BM dissociating water to transport protons and hydroxide ions through the membrane layers, enabling acid–base separation</cite>.
- Current efficiency and polarization control: <cite id="25b06b50-2">Approaching or exceeding LCD induces concentration polarization with high resistance, lower salt rejection, and reduced current efficiency; thus, current density must be controlled to avoid depletion of counter-ions at the diluate interface</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-3">LCD determines boundary-layer transport and mass-transport-limited operation; beyond threshold, water splitting raises current and reduces efficiency</cite>.
- Temperature affects ionic mobility, boundary-layer transport, and membrane properties. <cite id="995d701f-2">Between 25 and 50 °C, SEC decreased 28%; between 50–75 °C, a modest 1.5% decrease was observed (possible due to non-linear conductivity and component resistivity changes); between 75–85 °C, SEC fell 23% with a 41% current-efficiency increase, though higher temperatures may increase co-ion transport and purity risks, warranting further study</cite>.

Module and process innovations
- Pulsed electric-field ED (PEF-ED) can lower SEC and mitigate polarization by introducing relaxation phases. <cite id="995d701f-3">Shifting from continuous to pulsed electric field in ED generally decreases SEC, especially at high current densities where polarization is severe; optimal pulse frequency thresholds lie around 0.02–0.05 Hz depending on operating current; reducing duty cycle yields moderate energy savings, while increasing duty reduces operating time; applying current during relaxation periods further reduces SEC without compromising throughput and attenuates concentration polarization</cite>.
- Staging and staged operation tailor the driving force and residence time per compartment to approach RO-like energy at optimized conditions. <cite id="de245b43-1">Multistage ED matched single-stage performance for 200–500 mM desalination but required at least four stages to reach 3.6 kWh/m3 for synthetic seawater, demonstrating that staging adapts driving force to stage-specific conditions at lower energy</cite>.
- Flow design and inter-electrode spacing influence water drag and ion/cosolute transport. <cite id="25b06b50-1">Increasing voltage increases ion migration and electroosmotic water movement; stack voltage and flow conditions were optimized to maximize Li+ concentration while limiting energy loss and undesired water co-migration</cite>.
- Integration with filtration and other separations: <cite id="995d701f-0">Recent electrodialytic developments include electroconvective vortices, pulsed electric fields, electrodeionization, and shock electrodialysis; ED combined with filtration membranes (EDFM) is proposed for eco-efficient circular-economy strategies</cite>.
- Thermal management and antiscalant strategies: <cite id="de245b43-0">Temperature increases reduce electrical resistance by ~2% per °C, lowering ED energy consumption; ED is compatible with renewable energy and small-scale deployment</cite> <cite id="995d701f-2">At 85 °C, SEC decreased 23% and current efficiency rose 41%, though co-ion transport increased, suggesting a trade-off between energy, selectivity, and membrane stability that requires careful optimization</cite>.

Variants and hybrid systems
- Electrodeionization (EDI): combines ED with ion-exchange to continuously regenerate resins and produce high-purity water; EDI modules are widely deployed for demineralization and are part of the broader ED family. <cite id="7ee2a26c-2">Electrodialysis deionization (EDI) integrates with CED/EED/BMED to achieve high-resistivity product water via electrostatic ion removal and in situ regeneration</cite>.
- Bipolar electrodialysis (BMED) and reverse electrodialysis (RED): BMED produces acids/bases from salts; RED harvests energy from salinity gradients and can be integrated with RO to reduce net energy. <cite id="7ee2a26c-0">BMED dissociates water across bipolar membranes to generate acid and base currents, enabling acid/base recovery and purification from salts</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Bipolar ED concentrated acids up to 51× (HCl) and 63× (H2SO4) and produced 9× concentrated NaOH with low impurity levels relative to feed</cite> <cite id="de245b43-3">Hybrid RO–RED/FO/PRO systems can approach 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 for seawater desalination by leveraging salinity-gradient energy, with ED/RED contributing electricity-driven separations in the 2–6 kWh/m3 range</cite>.
- Selective ED and fractionation: using monovalent-selective membranes enables fractionation of ions by valence (e.g., Li+/Mg2+), supporting downstream recovery of valuable metals and acids. <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Selective electrodialysis (SED) replaces standard CEM/AEM with monovalent-selective membranes to fractionate monovalent and divalent ions (e.g., Li+ vs. Mg2+), enabling separation of inorganic acids and metal ions and facilitating recovery from process streams</cite>.

Applications
- Desalination and brine management: <cite id="de245b43-0">ED has industrial heritage in seawater and brackish desalination; while advances in RO have reduced new ED plant deployment for seawater, ED remains competitive for certain waters (≈2.2–3.6 kWh/m3) and is easily renewable-powered</cite> <cite id="de245b43-1">For synthetic seawater, ED multistage achieved 3.6 kWh/m3 to 200 mM, but non-optimized setups can be double RO’s energy; staging mitigates driving-force losses</cite>.
- Environmental treatment and circular economy: <cite id="995d701f-0">Electrodialytic processes are promising for wastewater treatment, food preservation, bioactive compound production, organic acid extraction, and energy recovery, with emerging techniques (pulsed fields, electroconvective vortices, electrodeionization, shock ED) boosting interest</cite> <cite id="995d701f-4">ED is considered an advanced treatment for removing organic ions at ambient temperature/pressure without harmful chemicals, with demonstrated roles in minimal liquid discharge (MLD) and zero-liquid discharge (ZLD) systems to minimize brine discharge and recover water, minerals, salts, and metals</cite>.
- Industrial acid/base and nutrient recovery: <cite id="7ee2a26c-0">BMED has produced organic acids (e.g., salicylic acid) and is effective in wastewater treatment by generating acid/base streams in situ without waste streams</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Acid/base recovery via bipolar ED achieved high concentration factors with low impurity carryover, enabling resource value recovery from industrial effluents</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-2">ED processes are increasingly applied to recover nitrogen, phosphorus, precious metals, and organic compounds from byproducts, wastewaters, and brines</cite>.
- Battery material production and specialty separations: <cite id="995d701f-2">In membrane electrodialysis for lithium hydroxide (LiOH) production, SEC decreased 28% from 25–50 °C, ~1.5% from 50–75 °C, and 23% from 75–85 °C, with current efficiency 41% higher at 85 °C; temperature increases improved ionic mobility and boundary-layer diffusion but increased co-ion transport risks</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-0">Voltage/current density tuning governs ion removal and water quality; for Li+ concentration, 60 V maximized Li+ to 18.12 g/L while balancing energy loss and water migration</cite>.
- Pharmaceutical and toxic compound removal: <cite id="995d701f-4">ED has been used for removal of harmful metallic ions and organic ions such as 4-nitrophenol with high removal efficiency, compact installations, and short treatment times, operating without harmful reagents</cite>.

Limitations, challenges, and mitigation
- Concentrate polarization, co-ion permeation, and scaling: <cite id="25b06b50-2">Operation near or above LCD induces polarization with surface ion depletion/recovery cycles that raise resistance, reduce salt rejection, and lower current efficiency</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-3">Above LCD, water splitting at boundary layers increases total current while decreasing current efficiency due to hydroxide/oxide formation and added transport needs</cite>.
- Fouling and antiscalants: <cite id="995d701f-4">ED is compatible with ambient conditions and avoids chemical additives in many separations, but high salinity and hardness in brines elevate scaling risk; ED is often integrated in MLD/ZLD to manage brines and recover resources, yet must address energy and scaling challenges</cite>.
- Scale-up and real-life constraints: <cite id="995d701f-0">Despite promising new membrane phenomena (electroconvective vortices, pulsed fields, electrodeionization, shock ED) and market evolution, hurdles remain in scale-up and real-life conditions; integration into circular-economy strategies is growing but deployment challenges persist</cite>.
- Energy and selectivity trade-offs: <cite id="de245b43-1">Even optimized ED can exceed RO energy by twofold without deeper process intensification, highlighting the need for improved stack/module hydrodynamics, staging, and membrane selectivity</cite> <cite id="995d701f-2">Higher temperatures can cut SEC and improve current efficiency but may increase co-ion transport and purity risks, requiring membrane and operating point trade-offs</cite>.
- Emerging mitigation strategies: <cite id="995d701f-3">Pulsed electric-field ED reduces SEC by attenuating polarization and using relaxation cycles; tailored pulse frequency (~0.02–0.05 Hz) and duty cycles provide significant energy savings with minimal throughput loss, and applying low current during relaxation helps attenuate polarization while maintaining transport</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-0">Voltage/current-density control balances ion removal and energy loss; excess voltage increases both ion and water transport, risking unwanted dilute-side co-ion migration</cite>.
- Materials and membranes: <cite id="25b06b50-2">Recent anion-exchange membrane advances showed higher limiting current densities and better electrodialysis performance than commercial AEMs, enabling higher current densities with low area resistance and improved stability</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-2">Ion-exchange membrane research targets improved selectivity, stability, and resource recovery from complex wastewaters and brines within the broader ED family</cite>.

Practical takeaways and outlook
- ED is a versatile electro-membrane process for desalination, ion concentration, and electrochemical conversion, with demonstrated energy ranges from ~2.2 to 6.6 kWh/m3 depending on water type and system configuration, and compatibility with renewable energy and small modular deployments. <cite id="de245b43-0">Specific energy consumption spans 2.2–6.6 kWh/m3 across optimized and seawater conditions; ED is easy to couple to renewable electricity and suitable for small-scale and mobile systems</cite>.
- Advances in pulsed-field operation, staging, selective membranes (including monovalent-selective and multivalent rejection), and ED-RO hybrids are narrowing energy gaps and expanding applicability to circular-economy goals, wastewater treatment, and specialty separations. <cite id="995d701f-3">Pulsed electric-field ED can reduce energy via polarization mitigation and optimized pulse/duty parameters</cite> <cite id="de245b43-1">Staged ED adapts driving force and residence time to approach lower energy targets</cite> <cite id="7ee2a26c-1">Selective ED and BMED enable ion and acid/base fractionation and high-concentration recovery from industrial streams</cite> <cite id="de245b43-3">ED/RED-RO hybrids can push net SEC toward 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 by harvesting salinity-gradient energy</cite>.
- Key challenges remain in large-scale robustness, polarization/scaling control, and maintaining selectivity–energy trade-offs; continued progress in membrane materials, module hydrodynamics, and process integration is central to broader industrialization and ZLD/MLD deployments. <cite id="995d701f-0">Scale-up and real-life hurdles are significant despite promising new membrane phenomena and market development; integration into circular-economy strategies is accelerating but constrained by deployment issues</cite> <cite id="25b06b50-2">Limiting current and polarization management are essential to sustain salt rejection and current efficiency</cite>.

Notes on related electromembrane processes
- Electromembrane processes share the core physics of ion transport through charged membranes under electric fields and include ED, EDR, BMED, EDI, MCDI, and RED. <cite id="7ee2a26c-4">Electromembrane processes—ED, EDR (reversal), BMED, EDI, MCDI, and RED—share ion migration across charged membranes; reviews discuss scaling mitigation, mass-transfer enhancement, and hybrid process development, with critical analyses of RED-based energy production</cite>.
- Coupling ED with reverse osmosis, forward osmosis, or pressure-retarded osmosis is an active area to leverage hydraulic and electrochemical gradients for lower net energy and higher water recovery in brine management. <cite id="de245b43-3">Hybrids of RO with FO, RED, or PRO can approach SEC of 1.3–1.5 kWh/m3 for seawater by harnessing salinity-gradient energy, with ED/RED modules providing electricity-driven separations in 2–6 kWh/m3 ranges</cite>.

Title: Special Issue “Membrane Technologies for Sustainable Biofood Production Lines”
Snippet: They also discussed the particularities involving the separation of spent brewer's yeast protein hydrolysates by taking into account engineering, technical, and practical aspects of membrane processes. In addition, in a context of preserving and improving human health, Bazinet and Geoffroy [7] confirmed that electrodialytic processes are very promising perspectives. Indeed, these processes allow the treatment of water, preservation of food products, production of bioactive compounds having health benefits, extraction of organic acids, and recovery of energy from natural and waste waters with minimal environmental impact. Hence, the most recent developments based on electrodialytic membrane phenomena such as applications of electroconvective vortices, use of pulsedelectric field, electrodeionization and shock electrodialysis are discussed. Additionally, the authors provided a global overview of the actual electrodialytic equipment market and manufacturers. 

Finally, the use of electrodialysis processes in sustainable strategies or in the framework of a circular economy are presented. The circular economy is an economy that operates in a loop, consequently avoiding the notion of waste and its objective is to produce goods while strongly limiting the consumption of raw materials and non-renewable energy sources. Hence, in their review, Bazinet and Geoffroy [7] give a global portrait of the most recent uses or potential uses of electrodialytic membrane processes in sustainable strategies. For this purpose, the authors mainly focused on articles reported in the literature from 2015 to June 2020. Based on these new developments or technologies, the authors presented and proposed the integration of electrodialytic technologies in sustainable strategies or use of eco-efficient new electrodialytic technologies such as electrodialysis with filtration membrane (EDFM). It appeared that new knowledge on pulsed electric fields, electroconvective vortices, overlimiting conditions, and reversal modes, as well as recent demonstrations of their applications, are currently boosting the interest for electrodialytic processes. However, the hurdles are still high when dealing with scale-ups and real-life conditions. In their papers, Abou Diab et al. [5,8] developed and proposed a new green application of EDBM to the production of bioactive peptides from a by-product of slaughterhouses, which fits perfectly with the concept of a circular economy.

Title: Trade-Off between Operating Time and Energy Consumption in Pulsed Electric Field Electrodialysis: A Comprehensive Simulation Study
Snippet: In this work, the effect of the input signal parameters on the performance of pulsed electric field electrodialysis has been systematically evaluated using a facile simulation model solved applying finite element methods. Different parameters, such as pulse frequency, duty cycle or applied current density in both the pulse and relaxation phases have been evaluated in terms of the specific energy consumption and operating time needed to achieve a constant transport of charges through the membranes. In general, it can be concluded that changing from continuous to PEF modes implies a general decrease in specific energy consumption; being this improvement more significant at high current densities, where high degrees of polarization are reached. There is a threshold frequency value from which further improvements in energy consumption become almost negligible. This frequency depends on the level of applied current i high , taking a value of 0.02 Hz for 0.7·i lim and increasing up to 0.05 Hz for 1.2·i lim . Decreasing the duty cycle provides moderate savings in energy consumption, while increasing it implies significant reductions in the operating time needed for a given desalination process. For the first time, a novel type of PEF function with application of current during the relaxation periods has been evaluated. These new PEF modes are found to be a promising strategy to effectively reduce the specific energy consumption, without compromising the operating time of ED processes. Application of low levels of current density during the relaxation periods is useful for attenuating concentration polarization, while maintaining ion transport during the entire ED operating time.

Title: Electrodialysis as a potential technology for 4-nitrophenol abatement from wastewater
Snippet: For several decades, electrodialysis (ED) has been widely used for the isolation of chemical compounds dissolved in water, such as water desalination, acid concentrations, mineral recovery, and removal of harmful metallic ions (Danaeifar et al. 2023;Li et al. 2023;Lotfy et al. 2022;Martí-Calatayud et al. 2012;Pramanik et al. 2017;Tian et al. 2021), among others. In these processes, its relevance is attributed to both its removal efficiency and its main operative advantages, including compact installations and short treatment times (Chang et al. 2010;Lotfy et al. 2022). In environmental terms, it is considered advanced, since it allows the removal of organic ions by innocuous processes, carried out at room temperature and pressure and without the addition of harmful chemical compounds (Bernardes et al. 2014;Rajoria et al. 2022). 

About a new promising application, the ED can be included as a technological step in novel integral processes known as minimal (MLD) or zero liquid discharge (ZLD), whose main purpose is the pollution control for environmental and human health protection (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2023). These systems address the elimination or minimization the brine discharge, from natural and industrial brine effluents, and recover valuable resources such as water, minerals, salts, and metals, among others. Technologies such as reverse osmosis (RO), forward osmosis (FO), brine concentrator (BC), and brine crystallizer (BCr), among others, also can be considered in these processes (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2022a). However, this must still overcome several drawbacks associated with the high energy consumption, emerging scale, and employment of fossil fuels as energy sources, among others (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2022b). In this context, the ED is an adequate choice to contemplate in these systems since it has been used industrially on a large scale for several decades.

Indeed, these processes allow the treatment of water, preservation of food products, production of bioactive compounds having health benefits, extraction of organic acids, and recovery of energy from natural and waste waters with minimal environmental impact. Hence, the most recent developments based on electrodialytic membrane phenomena such as applications of electroconvective vortices, use of pulsedelectric field, electrodeionization and shock electrodialysis are discussed. Additionally, the authors provided a global overview of the actual electrodialytic equipment market and manufacturers. 

Finally, the use of electrodialysis processes in sustainable strategies or in the framework of a circular economy are presented. The circular economy is an economy that operates in a loop, consequently avoiding the notion of waste and its objective is to produce goods while strongly limiting the consumption of raw materials and non-renewable energy sources. Hence, in their review, Bazinet and Geoffroy [7] give a global portrait of the most recent uses or potential uses of electrodialytic membrane processes in sustainable strategies. For this purpose, the authors mainly focused on articles reported in the literature from 2015 to June 2020. Based on these new developments or technologies, the authors presented and proposed the integration of electrodialytic technologies in sustainable strategies or use of eco-efficient new electrodialytic technologies such as electrodialysis with filtration membrane (EDFM). It appeared that new knowledge on pulsed electric fields, electroconvective vortices, overlimiting conditions, and reversal modes, as well as recent demonstrations of their applications, are currently boosting the interest for electrodialytic processes. However, the hurdles are still high when dealing with scale-ups and real-life conditions. In their papers, Abou Diab et al. [5,8] developed and proposed a new green application of EDBM to the production of bioactive peptides from a by-product of slaughterhouses, which fits perfectly with the concept of a circular economy.

documents.title: Trade-Off between Operating Time and Energy Consumption in Pulsed Electric Field Electrodialysis: A Comprehensive Simulation Study
documents.snippet: In this work, the effect of the input signal parameters on the performance of pulsed electric field electrodialysis has been systematically evaluated using a facile simulation model solved applying finite element methods. Different parameters, such as pulse frequency, duty cycle or applied current density in both the pulse and relaxation phases have been evaluated in terms of the specific energy consumption and operating time needed to achieve a constant transport of charges through the membranes. In general, it can be concluded that changing from continuous to PEF modes implies a general decrease in specific energy consumption; being this improvement more significant at high current densities, where high degrees of polarization are reached. There is a threshold frequency value from which further improvements in energy consumption become almost negligible. This frequency depends on the level of applied current i high , taking a value of 0.02 Hz for 0.7·i lim and increasing up to 0.05 Hz for 1.2·i lim . Decreasing the duty cycle provides moderate savings in energy consumption, while increasing it implies significant reductions in the operating time needed for a given desalination process. For the first time, a novel type of PEF function with application of current during the relaxation periods has been evaluated. These new PEF modes are found to be a promising strategy to effectively reduce the specific energy consumption, without compromising the operating time of ED processes. Application of low levels of current density during the relaxation periods is useful for attenuating concentration polarization, while maintaining ion transport during the entire ED operating time.

documents.title: Electrodialysis as a potential technology for 4-nitrophenol abatement from wastewater
documents.snippet:
For several decades, electrodialysis (ED) has been widely used for the isolation of chemical compounds dissolved in water, such as water desalination, acid concentrations, mineral recovery, and removal of harmful metallic ions (Danaeifar et al. 2023;Li et al. 2023;Lotfy et al. 2022;Martí-Calatayud et al. 2012;Pramanik et al. 2017;Tian et al. 2021), among others. In these processes, its relevance is attributed to both its removal efficiency and its main operative advantages, including compact installations and short treatment times (Chang et al. 2010;Lotfy et al. 2022). In environmental terms, it is considered advanced, since it allows the removal of organic ions by innocuous processes, carried out at room temperature and pressure and without the addition of harmful chemical compounds (Bernardes et al. 2014;Rajoria et al. 2022). 

About a new promising application, the ED can be included as a technological step in novel integral processes known as minimal (MLD) or zero liquid discharge (ZLD), whose main purpose is the pollution control for environmental and human health protection (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2023). These systems address the elimination or minimization the brine discharge, from natural and industrial brine effluents, and recover valuable resources such as water, minerals, salts, and metals, among others. Technologies such as reverse osmosis (RO), forward osmosis (FO), brine concentrator (BC), and brine crystallizer (BCr), among others, also can be considered in these processes (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2022a). However, this must still overcome several drawbacks associated with the high energy consumption, emerging scale, and employment of fossil fuels as energy sources, among others (Panagopoulos and Giannika 2022b). In this context, the ED is an adequate choice to contemplate in these systems since it has been used industrially on a large scale for several decades.

Snippet: Figure 7A illustrates that at a voltage of 60 V the maximum concentration of Li + reaches 18.12 g/L, indicating that this voltage provides an optimal driving force for Li + migration and concentration. Figure 7B illustrates that energy consumption exhibits a direct positive correlation with the applied voltage, as higher voltages increase current flow and consequently lead to greater ohmic losses across the membrane stack. Figure 7C illustrates that water migration in electrodialysis primarily occurs through electroosmotic drag accompanying ion transport, and increasing the voltage enhances both ion migration rates and the associated water movement [44]. Based on a comprehensive analysis of the voltage effects on concentration efficiency, energy consumption, and water migration amount, 60 V was selected as the optimal operating voltage for subsequent experiments. This determination reflects a balanced optimization among competing factors: while higher voltages enhance Li + concentration they also result in disproportionate increases in energy consumption and undesirable water migration. The 60 V condition achieves a significant Li + concentration (18.12 g/L) while maintaining acceptable energy efficiency and minimizing excessive water migration. This optimization approach aligns with established electrodialysis principles, where operational parameters are adjusted to maximize separation efficiency while minimizing energy consumption [45].

Title: Assessment of Graphical Methods for Determination of the Limiting Current Density in Complex Electrodialysis-Feed Solutions
Snippet: Electrodialysis (ED) is an electro-membrane ion separation process widely used to demineralize, concentrate, and/or convert salt-containing solutions [1][2][3][4]. Moreover, ED appears as an emerging technology for nutrient recovery in wastewater treatment [5][6][7][8]. The driving force for the salt separation is the application of an electrical potential across an ED membrane stack, whereby charged particles are removed from the feed solution. An ED membrane stack comprises alternately placed cation-and anion-exchange membranes. During ED, the feed stream is separated into two streams, one with a reduced concentration of ions (diluate), and the other enriched with ions (concentrate). From the techno-economical point of view, it is important to run ED under optimal operating conditions [9][10][11][12]. Various parameters, such as feed solution composition, temperature, flow, membrane characteristics, spacers, applied power, and current density, impact the ED process efficiency [2,[13][14][15][16][17][18]. One of the core parameters for the ED process design is the limiting current density (LCD) [19][20][21][22][23]. The experimentally determined LCD is commonly used for deriving the process essential boundary layer thickness, and it is directly proportional to the ion concentration and diffusivity [20,22,24]. The boundary layer is a thin layer of the solution adjacent to the membrane surface, with a concentration decrease of counter-ions on the diluate side and a concentration increase of co-ions on the concentrate side, compared to the bulk concentration [16]. The LCD indicates the electric current density that leads to the depletion of ions in the boundary layer on the diluate side, as a result of the concentration polarization [24]. With a further increase of the current density above a certain threshold, a dissociation of water molecules to H + and OH − ions occurs in the boundary layer as an undesired effect, causing an increase of the overall current density and subsequently a decrease in the current efficiency.

Title: Class II (three-layer system) phenomenological model based on limiting current density and dynamic chelation chemistry for separation of rare earth elements using electrodialysis
Snippet: This expression is crucial for understanding the conditions under which electrodialysis processes achieve their maximum efficiency, particularly in systems utilizing strongly charged cation exchange membranes. It serves as a fundamental basis for optimizing the transport dynamics and overall performance of electrodialysis systems in separating and concentrating ions from multi-ionic solutions. 

A similar approach can be taken for a strongly charged anion exchange membrane: The limiting transport numbers of the counterions, which indicate the point at which the limiting current density is achieved for both cation and anion exchange membranes, are described by Eqs. ( 12), (13), following the linearized Nernst-Planck methodology. It is important to emphasize that this specific set of limiting transport numbers is distinctive and remains consistent across any mass-transport model utilized within the membranes. 

These limiting transport numbers are derived under an asymptotic condition where all ionic concentrations approach zero but do not exactly reach nullity. When the concentrations of all ions are zero, Eq. (10) becomes inapplicable for calculating i lim because, under such circumstances, the product C j,m ξ m does not equate to zero in Eq. (7). Instead, with C j,m = 0 inserted into Eq. ( 7), a new formula is derived for C j,m ξ m , providing a basis for understanding the behavior of ionic transport at the threshold of the limiting current density, where traditional calculations based on concentration gradients and potential differences need to be re-evaluated. 

By combining Eq. ( 14) with Eq. ( 8) (the electroneutrality) and rearranging, we can obtain the equation for i lim : 

This equation results in different limiting current densities for cation and anion exchange membranes, with the outcome being positive for the cation exchange membrane and negative for the anion exchange membrane, in alignment with the established coordinate system (x). In practical applications, the limiting current density is determined by selecting the lowest among the absolute values calculated for each type of membrane. This approach ensures the identification of the operational threshold that prevents excessive ion depletion or concentration polarization, thereby optimizing the effectiveness and stability of the electrodialysis process.

When the concentrations of all ions are zero, Eq. (10) becomes inapplicable for calculating i lim because, under such circumstances, the product C j,m ξ m does not equate to zero in Eq. (7). Instead, with C j,m = 0 inserted into Eq. ( 7), a new formula is derived for C j,m ξ m , providing a basis for understanding the behavior of ionic transport at the threshold of the limiting current density, where traditional calculations based on concentration gradients and potential differences need to be re-evaluated. 

By combining Eq. ( 14) with Eq. ( 8) (the electroneutrality) and rearranging, we can obtain the equation for i lim : 

This equation results in different limiting current densities for cation and anion exchange membranes, with the outcome being positive for the cation exchange membrane and negative for the anion exchange membrane, in alignment with the established coordinate system (x). In practical applications, the limiting current density is determined by selecting the lowest among the absolute values calculated for each type of membrane. This approach ensures the identification of the operational threshold that prevents excessive ion depletion or concentration polarization, thereby optimizing the effectiveness and stability of the electrodialysis process.

Title: Experimental investigation of multistage electrodialysis for seawater desalination
Snippet: Abstract Electrodialysis (ED) is currently used for selective removal of ions and brackish water desalination, while for seawater desalination ED is considered to be too energy intensive. This research focuses on the viability of ED using multiple stages for seawater desalination. With staging, the driving force is adapted to the governing conditions at that specific stage, operating at its individual optimum at lower energy consumption. An ED multistage configuration is examined that contains up to four stages. We compare single stage with multistage ED and investigate the effect of operation parameters. Different current densities are applied and optimized and residence time is compared to describe both transmembrane salt and water fluxes. We showed that desalination from 500 mM to 200 mM is possible, but that for these desalination conditions a multistage and single-stage system perform equal. Operation of each stage of the multistage close to limiting current density shows that desalination of synthetic seawater close to drinking water quality is possible. To reach this, the energy consumption is 3.6 kWh/m3 and at least 4 stages are needed. Although outlet concentrations between ED and RO are different, this non-optimized ED system showed double the energy consumption of the state-of-the-art desalination technology RO.

Title: Economic and Reliability Assessment of Hybrid PRO-RO Desalination Systems Using Brine for Salinity Gradient Energy Production
Snippet: In comparison, membrane desalination methods use membranes with unique chemical and physical properties, and examples of membrane desalination methods include: electrodialysis, forward osmosis, electrodialysis reversal, membrane distillation, nano-filtration, PRO and RO [9]. Thermal processes require both thermal and electrical energy; thus, they are highly energyintensive, with specific energy consumption (SEC) ranging from 5.5 to about 27 kWh/m 3 . The membrane processes usually required only electrical energy or pressure differences for desalination, with SEC ranging between 2 to 6 kWh/m 3 . Despite the lower energy requirement of membrane processes, all desalination techniques have their peculiar limitations and share a common challenge of brine management. 

Despite being the most reliable membrane method of seawater desalination, RO is faced with membrane fouling and some soluble rejection efficacy. Improvement on RO systems has led to extensive research on membrane development using nanomaterials [16][17][18]. In addition, several studies have suggested the hybrid of RO and other desalination methods to improve performance. The authors of [13,14,19] designed a model that combined RO, ED, and crystallization methods to achieve salt production and minimize brine production from seawater desalination. The cost and energy requirements of the systems were examined and prove to be economically viable and fit for brine management, but the capital and operational costs of ED and crystallization were not considered in the economic analysis. 

Hybridization of RO with either forward osmosis (FO), reverse electrodialysis (RED), or PRO is considered very promising, since the three (FO, RED, and PRO) are major technologies that utilize ocean salinity gradient energy. The authors of [20][21][22] present the hybrid of FO-RO technologies and evaluate the system's performance and economic viability. It was suggested that the FO-RO hybrid could approach a SEC threshold of 1.3-1.5 kWh/m 3 for seawater desalination using a FO membrane of about 10 L/m 3 [20]. This hybrid process reduces energy demand and freshwater cost and reduces the environmental impact of brine.

Title: Study of the Seawater Desalination Performance by Electrodialysis
Snippet: They discovered that the removal of calcium and magnesium was greater for both CEMs compared with the removal of sodium and that operating at low current density had no impact. The multivalent ion permeable CEMs allowed for the removal of more magnesium [12]. 

Moreover, the removal of the nitrate, arsenic and fluoride by electrodialysis from brackish groundwater were also investigated by Aliaskari et al. [13]. In this study, a batch electrodialysis system was used to explore the effects of operational (flowrate and electricpotential) and water quality (salinity, contaminant feed concentration and pH) factors on brackish water decontamination. However, the composition of the saline groundwater used in the study differed somewhat from that of seawater. 

In summary, studies in the literature on electrodialysis desalination have focused on setting up experiments to investigate the factors affecting the desalination process and the operational performance of electrodialysis desalination. However, few studies have discussed the factors influencing desalination performance comprehensively. In this work, the ion removal efficiency and mass transfer flux of the whole module of the desalination process are experimentally calculated, and the major and minor factors affecting the desalination process are quantitatively analysed.

Title: Innovations in electromembrane processes
Snippet: Electromembrane processes are increasingly important group of separation methods, widely used for removal of charged components from solutions. It is a growing field of research with a plethora of both existing and still developed applications. The separation is based on ion migration across the charged membranes (a polymeric matrix with fixed charged groups, counterbalanced with mobile counter-ions), placed in the electric field. This paper presents the main electromembrane processes: electrodialysis (ED), electrodialysis reversal (EDR), electrodialysis with bipolar membrane (EDBM), electrodeionization (EDI), membrane capacitive deionization (MCDI), reverse electrodialysis (RED). We present the common applications of electromembrane processes and discuss the physical basis of the electromembrane processes. The most important parameters of the ion-exchange membranes are discussed, as well as the novel approaches towards mitigation of scaling, enhancement of mass transfer, decreasing the concentration polarization, and new hybrid electromembrane processes. Critical analysis of the possibility of energy production by reverse electrodialysis is presented.

snippet.text: Electromembrane processes are increasingly important group of separation methods, widely used for removal of charged components from solutions. It is a growing field of research with a plethora of both existing and still developed applications. The separation is based on ion migration across the charged membranes (a polymeric matrix with fixed charged groups, counterbalanced with mobile counter-ions), placed in the electric field. This paper presents the main electromembrane processes: electrodialysis (ED), electrodialysis reversal (EDR), electrodialysis with bipolar membrane (EDBM), electrodeionization (EDI), membrane capacitive deionization (MCDI), reverse electrodialysis (RED). We present the common applications of electromembrane processes and discuss the physical basis of the electromembrane processes. The most important parameters of the ion-exchange membranes are discussed, as well as the novel approaches towards mitigation of scaling, enhancement of mass transfer, decreasing the concentration polarization, and new hybrid electromembrane processes. Critical analysis of the possibility of energy production by reverse electrodialysis is presented.
