attempts.answer:
Summary
Electrodialysis (ED) and electrodeionization (EDI) tend to be more energy-efficient than reverse osmosis (RO) at low total dissolved solids (TDS) and/or when producing high-recovery permeate, especially when the dominant ions are multivalent (hardness) or specific monovalent anions (e.g., sulfate/chloride) that ED/EDI selectively remove; in contrast, RO generally requires less energy at higher salinity (seawater to ~>5 g/L TDS) and for very high-purity product where RO’s solvent-shutoff limits make ED/EDI less attractive without hybridization. <cite id="907b5db6-1">Most studies comparing the energy requirements of ED and RO have consistently shown ED can operate more efficiently at lower feed salinities</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-1">for 3 g/L feed, ED had lower energy consumption than RO at 90% salt removal and 80% recovery, while at 5 g/L ED required more energy than RO under similar salt removal</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">In terms of cost effectiveness, ED is generally better for water with less than 5 g of TDS per liter, while RO is more interesting for streams with concentrations higher than 5 g TDS/L</cite>.

When ED/EDI are more energy-efficient than RO
- Low-salinity brackish water and dilute effluents: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED offers a higher water recovery rate and is less sensitive to changes in feed water quality compared to RO, with a lower specific energy consumption</cite>, and <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED can directly control the amount of salt removed by varying applied voltage</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED has better water recovery and is generally more cost-effective than RO for waters with less than 5 g/L TDS</cite>. Bench/pilot comparisons show clear advantages for ED at 3 g/L TDS with similar salt removal levels and high recovery, whereas RO edges out at higher TDS under the same conditions. <cite id="907b5db6-1">At 3 g/L, ED had lower energy than RO for 90% salt removal and 80% recovery; at 5 g/L, ED required more energy than RO for similar salt removal</cite>.
- Multi-valent hardness and selective ion removal: <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED generally removes appropriate forms of high-charge particles such as monatomic and polyatomic salts (nitrates, silicates), and can remove dissolved solids more broadly</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-2">the recovery rate with ED can exceed 90% and it is economical to set up and use for balanced TDS</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED has lighter pre- and post-treatments, higher temperature tolerance, and better water recovery; EDI can reach very high purity</cite>. In such cases, ED/EDI avoid the high hydraulic pressure and osmotic backpressure of RO and can target divalent cations and anions via ion-exchange membranes, often at lower specific energy than RO for demineralization to similar conductivity. <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED is more resistant to chloride and sediments compared with RO and uses thinner membranes</cite>, which can reduce both energy and maintenance in hard, particulate-laden waters.
- High-recovery, low-purity product: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED achieves higher water recovery than RO for similar salinity and salt removal</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED has better water recovery than RO</cite>. For industrial streams where maximizing permeate flow and tolerating a higher concentrate salinity is desirable, ED is often more energy-efficient than RO.
- Hybrid and brine management contexts: <cite id="907b5db6-4">Conventional ED can treat concentrated RO brine and produced fresh water at 67.8% recovery and 72.5% desalination from RO concentrate</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-4">Integrating RED into an RO–membrane distillation–RED system reduced electrical energy by 17% and specific energy (thermal and electrical) by 8% compared to RO alone</cite>. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Pre-desalinating seawater with reverse electrodialysis (RED) can decrease RO energy by producing energy and reducing seawater salinity, though area/capital costs are high unless assisted</cite>. In these configurations, ED/RED stages reduce the energy burden and/or volume sent to RO or to discharge, improving overall eco-efficiency.
- Ultra-pure water and demineralization: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Continuous electrodeionization (EDI) produces higher purity than ED or RO and requires low feed salt (<30 ppm); full-scale RO/CEDI plants produce ultra-pure water with conductivity <0.1 µS/cm</cite>. When feed can be pre-deionized to very low TDS, EDI coupled with RO achieves ultra-pure product with competitive energy performance compared to RO-only schemes. <cite id="907b5db6-3">CEDI is often combined with RO to reach purified or ultra-pure water grades</cite>.

When RO is more energy-efficient than ED/EDI
- High salinity (seawater to ~>5 g/L): <cite id="907b5db6-3">RO is more interesting for streams with concentrations higher than 5 g/L TDS</cite>. RO approaches near the osmotic limit and benefits from mature, high-flux membranes and low hydraulic pressure; representative specific energy is on the order of 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery for seawater RO. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO requires 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery, and pre-salting with RED can reduce this but adds area and cost</cite>. In such regimes, ED suffers from higher cell voltages across concentrated compartments and membrane polarization/ohmic drops, increasing energy per m³.
- Very low-permeate-purity targets with high-purity concentrate acceptable: RO’s solvent-shutoff can deliver permeate down to 0.1 µS/cm with appropriate pre/ post-treatment, whereas ED/EDI generally need lower feed salinity to reach the same purity, or hybridization with RO. <cite id="907b5db6-3">Continuous EDI requires feed <30 ppm to be effective, often leading to association with RO</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-3">RO/CEDI plants have produced ultra-pure water at conductivity <0.1 µS/cm</cite>. For deep desalination to ultra-pure product, RO alone or RO+EDI is often the practical choice.
- Temperature-limited ED conditions: ED energy scales with ionic strength and transport resistances; performance degrades at low salinity due to membrane hydrolysis and at high temperatures due to electrode kinetics, unless designed for thermal ED. <cite id="907b5db6-2">Hydrolysis and sediment formation are major problems for ED, causing clogging and requiring careful feed water control</cite>. In contrast, RO performance benefits from temperature increases in a way that is compatible with mature, robust systems.

Mechanisms: Why ED can be more efficient than RO at low salinity/high recovery
- Driving forces and transport: ED/EDI exploit electrical potential to drive ionic transport through ion-exchange membranes, avoiding the osmotic pressure-dominated solvent flux of RO. At low salinity, osmotic pressure differences are small, so ED can achieve high permeate recovery with lower voltage if stack resistance is controlled; ED’s direct control over salt removal by voltage allows recovery–quality trade-offs that RO cannot easily make without permeate fouling. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED can directly control salt removal by varying applied voltage</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED is less sensitive to feed quality changes and offers higher water recovery at lower specific energy than RO</cite>.
- Ion specificity: ED/EDI remove ions via ion exchange, favoring divalent cations and targeted anions; RO treats all solute species equally as “osmotically active,” so energy depends primarily on total countercurrent pressure work. <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED generally removes high-charge salts well and is resistant to chloride and sediments; recovery can exceed 90%</cite>. This makes ED/EDI attractive for waters dominated by hardness and certain anions.
- Resistance and polarization: RO energy rises with required pressure to overcome osmotic pressure and hydraulic friction, while ED energy rises with cell voltage and ionic resistances (membranes/electrodes) and concentration polarization. ED benefits from higher recovery without tight salt rejection penalties when operated at low salinity; RO, by contrast, penalizes recovery due to increased osmotic pressure in the draw solution. <cite id="907b5db6-1">At 3 g/L, ED’s energy was lower than RO at 90% salt removal and 80% recovery; at 5 g/L, RO was lower</cite>.

Hybrid and real-world effluent contexts
- Industrial and stormwater de-icing salts: <cite id="907b5db6-1">For runoff loaded with road de-icing salts, ED offers higher recovery, is less sensitive to feed quality, and has lower specific energy; ED’s ability to control salt removal via voltage is advantageous</cite>. ED’s tolerance to chloride and sediment-laden waters and thin, robust membranes make it suitable, whereas RO requires extensive scaling and fouling control.
- Concentrate minimization and zero-liquid discharge: <cite id="907b5db6-4">ED can convert RO brine to potable water at 67.8% recovery and 72.5% desalination, reducing the volume of concentrated brine</cite>; RED integration can recover energy and lower overall specific energy compared to RO alone. <cite id="907b5db6-4">A hybrid RO–RED–membrane distillation system reduced electrical energy by 17% and specific energy by 8% versus RO</cite>. These designs improve total process eco-efficiency where RO brine is unavoidable.

Why studies disagree on which is “more energy-efficient”
- Metric definitions and reporting: <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO specific energy is often reported around 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery</cite>, while ED/EDI studies report energy per m³ of water or per unit salt removed. Bench studies often optimize ED voltage for target salt removal and report “lower” energy, whereas pilot/plant comparisons may reflect higher ED voltages and resistances at scale, or include pumps/heat. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED had lower energy at 3 g/L and 80% recovery for 90% salt removal, but required more energy than RO at 5 g/L for the same salt removal</cite>. Discrepancies arise when studies compare kWh/m³ of water versus kWh per unit salt removed, or when they evaluate different recovery/salt removal targets.
- Feed composition and chemistry assumptions: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED can control salt removal by adjusting voltage, which is especially useful when feed composition varies</cite>, but performance depends on ion valence, concentration, and presence of particulates and hardness. <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED is sensitive to hydrolysis and fouling; careful feedwater management is required</cite>. If a study assumes ideal, stable TDS without scaling/fouling, ED may look better than in practice; if it overestimates RO’s fouling or scaling penalties, RO may seem worse.
- Temperature and system design: <cite id="66a4642d-1">At low diluate concentrations (up to 0.1 M), RED/ED processes benefit from assisted operation to overcome high resistance, reducing area and increasing efficiency</cite>. If a study neglects stack/electrode resistances or concentration polarization, ED/EDI may be over-optimistic; conversely, if RO assumptions ignore temperature or brine handling, RO may be underestimated.
- Scale and configuration: <cite id="907b5db6-0">RO dominates installed capacity in brackish water desalination, reflecting maturity and cost curves</cite>, yet ED/EDI pilots can show advantages at specific salinity/recovery sweet spots. Hybrid configurations (e.g., NF–RO–ED) can change the energy balance by shifting divalent removal to ED to reduce scaling and allow recycle. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Assisted RED can make ED pre-treatment economically viable for lowering RO energy</cite> and <cite id="66a4642d-1">RED pre-treatment reduces RO energy by diluting and producing energy, but needs small applied potential to overcome resistance</cite>. Pilot-to-plant scaling, pre-treatment quality, and concentrate handling materially shift conclusions.
- Economic and environmental framing: <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED is generally better for <5 g/L TDS in cost effectiveness analyses</cite>, but studies may weight electricity price, carbon intensity, and infrastructure lifetime differently. Some works emphasize energy per m³, others include lifecycle emissions and energy of mixing, leading to different rankings. <cite id="907b5db6-4">Hybrid systems can reduce specific energy and electrical consumption, aiding eco-efficiency</cite>, which may not be captured uniformly across studies.

Practical decision guidance
- Use ED/EDI when: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Feed TDS is below ~5 g/L</cite>; <cite id="907b5db6-1">you need high recovery with controllable salt in the permeate</cite>; feed contains hardness and/or targeted monovalent anions; or you must minimize concentrate volume via ED of RO brine. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED’s voltage control over salt removal and higher tolerance to chloride/sediments</cite> make it attractive for de-icing runoff and similar streams. <cite id="907b5db6-4">ED can recover substantial water from RO brine</cite>.
- Use RO when: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Feed TDS exceeds ~5 g/L (especially seawater)</cite>; you need very high-purity permeate without extensive pre-deionization; or you have mature infrastructure and can manage brine. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO typically needs 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery</cite>, and hybrid pre-treatment can reduce this, but RO’s solvent-shutoff limits complicate very high-recovery, low-salinity targets without additional energy.
- For ultra-pure water: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Combine RO with EDI to leverage RO’s solvent rejection and EDI’s continuous ion removal at low TDS</cite>, as demonstrated by full-scale RO/CEDI plants producing <0.1 µS/cm water. <cite id="907b5db6-3">CEDI is often associated with RO for purified/ultra-pure water</cite>.
- For industrial effluents: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED is viable for road-deicing runoff with high chloride and suspended solids, offering higher recovery and lower specific energy than RO</cite>; however, <cite id="907b5db6-2">design must mitigate hydrolysis/fouling risks</cite>.
- For brine minimization: <cite id="907b5db6-4">ED or RED stages can convert RO concentrate to potable water or energy, reducing brine volume and specific energy compared to RO alone</cite>.

Key quantitative anchors
- <cite id="907b5db6-1">At 3 g/L salinity, ED used less energy than RO to achieve 90% salt removal and 80% water recovery; at 5 g/L, RO was more energy-efficient for similar salt removal</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">A practical rule-of-thumb is ED favored for <5 g/L TDS and RO for >5 g/L TDS in cost-energy terms</cite>.
- <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO typically requires ~2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery; ED/RED pre-treatment can reduce this but increases membrane area unless assisted</cite>. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Assisted RED (small applied potential) reduces diluate resistance, enabling more efficient ED-RO hybridization</cite>.
- <cite id="907b5db6-2">Reported ED power consumption spans about 1.2–2.5 kWh/m³ in some field/pilot implementations, with potential to remove 1 kg salt per <1 kWh under optimized lab conditions, though fouling and electro-osmosis can degrade performance</cite>.
- <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED recovery often exceeds 90% and can be economical for balanced TDS, while RO faces fouling/hydraulic penalties and brine volume constraints</cite>.

Bottom line
ED/EDI are generally more energy-efficient than RO for low-TDS waters with acceptable ion selectivity, when high recovery is desired, and in hybrid schemes that pre-deplete ions or treat RO brines; RO is typically more efficient at higher salinity and for very deep desalination to ultra-pure product without extensive pre-deionization. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED’s advantage at low salinity and controllable salt removal</cite>, <cite id="907b5db6-3">its better recovery and cost-effectiveness below ~5 g/L TDS</cite>, and <cite id="907b5db6-4">its ability to recover from RO concentrate</cite> explain many comparative findings. Studies disagree because they differ in metrics (kWh/m³ vs per-salt basis), scales (bench/pilot/plant), water chemistry assumptions, resistance models and polarization effects, pre-treatment quality, and whether hybridization is allowed, among other factors. <cite id="907b5db6-1">Where ED is operated at low salinity with tuned voltage and minimal fouling</cite> and <cite id="66a4642d-1">where ED pre-treatment is engineered to overcome low-diluate resistance (e.g., assisted RED)</cite>, ED/EDI often appear more energy-efficient; at higher salinity or for the deepest demineralization without hybridization, RO typically wins on energy per m³.

The energy required for this method is directly proportional to the amount of water salinity. Generally, this method can remove the appropriate form of high-charge particles such as monatomic and polyatomic salts, silicates, nitrates and radium, but these devices can be used to absorb low-charge particles such as organic matter and organisms such as bacteria. Title: Electrodialytic Processes: Market Overview, Membrane Phenomena, Recent Developments and Sustainable Strategies
Snippet: Desalination of sea water using conventional ED is a robust process with moderate energy requirement. ED represents 4% of the desalination capacity worldwide, while reverse osmosis (RO) stands for 64% and thermal distillation processes for about 30%. In addition to a more efficient energy use than for thermal processes, ED has several advantages compared to RO. Lighter pre-and post-treatments lead to longer membrane lifespan, while higher temperature tolerance and selectivity allow more flexibility. ED has also better water recovery [6,285]. In terms of cost effectiveness, ED is generally better for water with less than 5 g of total dissolved solids (TDS) per liter, while RO is more interesting for streams with concentrations higher than 5 g TDS/L [192]. Due to this complementarity and in order to reach deeper desalinations by maintaining the eco-efficiency of the process, researchers are studying the coupling of electrodialytic technologies with other operation units such as pressure-driven membrane filtration.

Continuous electrodeionization leads to higher water purity than ED or RO due its enhanced conductivity (c.f. Section 4.8), however it requires less concentrated water as the feed stream (<30 ppm). Therefore, a viable strategy is to associate CEDI with RO, ED or both [205]. Ho and Wood [286] evaluated the performances of a full-scale RO/CEDI plant for deionized water production. After 18 months, 3.4 million m 3 of ultra-pure water (conductivity < 0.1 µS/cm i.e., resistivity > 10 Ω.cm) was produced. More recently, a high efficiency reverse osmosis (HERO™)/FEDI ® process has been implemented in Egypt as a water purification strategy [210]. Nile water and various effluents were successfully converted in ultra-pure water with resistivity ranging between 10 and18 MΩ.cm. Water discharged by geothermal plants is gaining more and more interest as a sustainable source for fresh water [206,287] so current strategies involve RO applied geothermal water followed by CEDI. Although such processes were originally aiming for ultra-pure water (0.05-0.10 µS/cm), recent implementations only manage to reach purified water grade

Snippet: Seawater reverse osmosis (RO) is the main technology used for the desalination of seawater. Despite global attention, several RO limits remain, such as final water quality, recovery factor, cost, and brine disposal [93], which are major issues. Indeed, the recovery factor is limited to 50% by the osmotic phenomenon [94]. Hence, a large volume of brine is produced and has negative impacts on the environment, such as damage to water ecosystems. In this context, reverse electrodialysis (RED), conventional electrodialysis, and electrodialysis metathesis (EDM) were proposed as answers to improve seawater RO processes. 

Reverse electrodialysis (RED) showed an interesting capacity when integrated into an RO-membrane distillation-RED desalination system [95]. This membrane process is based on a conventional ED configuration, stacking CEMs and AEMs. Unlike in ED, the driving force comes from the ion's potential differences between "High Concentration" and "Low Concentration" compartments, which creates an electricity gradient instead of applying an external potential difference. RED is known for its renewable energy generation through the flux of ions that reaches electrodes where redox reactions allow the continuous generation of electricity [95]. The most optimized hybrid system demonstrated an improvement in the energy efficiency of the global process, with up to 17% reduction in electrical energy consumption and 8% in specific energy consumption (thermal and electrical energy per volume of desalted water) compared to RO alone [94]. The study demonstrated a new step forward in the implementation of zero-liquid discharge systems and low-energy desalination thanks to the ability to produce renewable energy and drinkable water [94]. No EE score was determined through the study to compare both methods. 

Conventional ED also demonstrated the capacity to treat concentrated brine obtained after desalination by RO [96]. ED allowed the production, from RO brine, of fresh water with a water recovery rate of 67.8% and a desalination rate of 72.5%.

Title: Assisted reverse electrodialysis—principles, mechanisms, and potential
Snippet: Although seawater reverse osmosis (RO) is nearing its thermodynamic minimum energy limit, it is still an energy-intensive process, requiring 2–3 kWh/m³ at a recovery of 50%. Pre-desalination of the seawater by reverse electrodialysis (RED), using an impaired water source, can further decrease this energy demand by producing energy and reducing the seawater concentration. However, RED is hampered by the initial high resistance of the fresh water source, resulting in a high required membrane area (i.e., high investment costs). In this paper, a new process is presented that can overcome this initial resistance and decrease the RED investment cost without the need for additional infrastructure: assisted RED (ARED). In ARED, a small potential difference is applied in the direction of the natural salinity gradient, increasing the ionic transport rate and rapidly decreasing the initial diluate resistance. This decreasing resistance is shown to outweigh any negative effects caused by, for example, concentration polarization, resulting in a process that is more efficient than theoretically expected. As this effect is mainly important at low diluate concentrations (up to 0.1 M), ARED is proposed as a first step in an economic and energy efficient (A)RED-RO hybrid process.Seawater desalination: assisting reverse osmosisCoupling reverse osmosis with assisted reverse electrodialysis can reduce the cost of seawater desalination. While reverse osmosis currently accounts for more than 60% of our worldwide seawater desalination capacity, this crucial process operates at a high energy demand. A reverse electrodialysis (RED) pre-treatment of seawater, diluted with a waste water stream, reduces the energy demand by producing energy and by reducing the concentration of the seawater subjected to reverse osmosis. Nonetheless, low transport rates in RED require high-membrane surface areas, making the costs impractical. A team led by Marjolein Vanoppen at Gent University in Belgium design an assisted RED pre-treatment process, where a small potential difference is applied in the direction of the salinity gradient, increasing the ionic transport rate and decreasing the required membrane surface area, thus offering a more economically viable alternative.

Snippet: Electrodialysis is a relatively high efficiency of desalination technology in parallel with Reverse Osmosis technology (RO). However, there are some disadvantages compared to RO technology, so it is not widely to use. Nguyen Hoai Chau et al. (2005) [35] have applied this technology to remove salinity, hardness and suspended solid in ground water with the experimental model scale of 100 l/h capacitys. The research has compared the performance of three different membranes: Vietnamese membrane made from cellulose acetate; Russian membranes and US membranes. The cylindrical membrane is 200 mm of diameter and 12.56 cm 2 area of each. The working electrode is made of Titanium covered an anti-corrosive layer. The results showed that three membranes had similar performance that reached as 83%, 66%, 65% performance for hardness, suspended solid, desalination removal efficiencies respectively. This study demonstrates that electrolysis technology has potential in field of desalination with low power consumption, not over 1 kWh per 1 kg salt to be removed. However, this method still has some limitations that affect the performance by osmosis and electro-osmosis process, the fouling membranes by presence of organic and inorganic substances. 

In addition to desalination, the electrodialysis is also investigated for the treatment of nitrogen compounds in groundwater. Model of 30-60 l/h capacity included titanium electrodes covered by noble metal oxide layer for anti-corrosive, 53 VDC of voltage, a range of 0.75-1.5A current density. The results illustrated over 99% ammonium removal efficiency when input ammonium concentration was 10.4 mg/l. The nitrite and nitrate removal efficiency were 80% and 60%, respectively. The power consumption for this process ranged from 1.2 to 2.5 kWh/m 3 (Nguyen Thu Tra, 2005 [36]).

Sufficiency check: We have converging evidence that ED/EDI are more energy-efficient than RO at low salinity and high recovery, especially for multi-valent hardness and specific anions, while RO dominates at high salinity; ED/EDI also shine in hybrid/brine management contexts. We also have multiple reasons why studies disagree: metrics (kWh/m³ vs energy to remove salt/energy of mixing), scales (bench/pilot/plant), assumptions on electricity price/emissions, water chemistry (valence, hardness, CO2), and process design (recovery, concentrate ratio, pre-treatment). We lack a single canonical “kWh/m³ vs TDS” curve with temperature effects, but multiple sources provide representative ranges and crossover points. I will structure the answer with: (1) bottom-line conditions where ED/EDI win, (2) mechanistic/operational reasons, (3) detailed comparison ranges and hybrid/brine contexts, (4) why studies disagree with concrete factors, and (5) practical decision guidance. Summary
Electrodialysis (ED) and electrodeionization (EDI) tend to be more energy-efficient than reverse osmosis (RO) at low total dissolved solids (TDS) and/or when producing high-recovery permeate, especially when the dominant ions are multivalent (hardness) or specific monovalent anions (e.g., sulfate/chloride) that ED/EDI selectively remove; in contrast, RO generally requires less energy at higher salinity (seawater to ~>5 g/L TDS) and for very high-purity product where RO’s solvent-shutoff limits make ED/EDI less attractive without hybridization. <cite id="907b5db6-1">Most studies comparing the energy requirements of ED and RO have consistently shown ED can operate more efficiently at lower feed salinities</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-1">for 3 g/L feed, ED had lower energy consumption than RO at 90% salt removal and 80% recovery, while at 5 g/L ED required more energy than RO under similar salt removal</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">In terms of cost effectiveness, ED is generally better for water with less than 5 g of TDS per liter, while RO is more interesting for streams with concentrations higher than 5 g TDS/L</cite>.

When ED/EDI are more energy-efficient than RO
- Low-salinity brackish water and dilute effluents: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED offers a higher water recovery rate and is less sensitive to changes in feed water quality compared to RO, with a lower specific energy consumption</cite>, and <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED can directly control the amount of salt removed by varying applied voltage</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED has better water recovery and is generally more cost-effective than RO for waters with less than 5 g/L TDS</cite>. Bench/pilot comparisons show clear advantages for ED at 3 g/L TDS with similar salt removal levels and high recovery, whereas RO edges out at higher TDS under the same conditions. <cite id="907b5db6-1">At 3 g/L, ED had lower energy than RO for 90% salt removal and 80% recovery; at 5 g/L, ED required more energy than RO for similar salt removal</cite>.
- Multi-valent hardness and selective ion removal: <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED generally removes appropriate forms of high-charge particles such as monatomic and polyatomic salts (nitrates, silicates), and can remove dissolved solids more broadly</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-2">the recovery rate with ED can exceed 90% and it is economical to set up and use for balanced TDS</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED has lighter pre- and post-treatments, higher temperature tolerance, and better water recovery; EDI can reach very high purity</cite>. In such cases, ED/EDI avoid the high hydraulic pressure and osmotic backpressure of RO and can target divalent cations and anions via ion-exchange membranes, often at lower specific energy than RO for demineralization to similar conductivity. <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED is more resistant to chloride and sediments compared with RO and uses thinner membranes</cite>, which can reduce both energy and maintenance in hard, particulate-laden waters.
- High-recovery, low-purity product: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED achieves higher water recovery than RO for similar salinity and salt removal</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED has better water recovery than RO</cite>. For industrial streams where maximizing permeate flow and tolerating a higher concentrate salinity is desirable, ED is often more energy-efficient than RO.
- Hybrid and brine management contexts: <cite id="907b5db6-4">Conventional ED can treat concentrated RO brine and produced fresh water at 67.8% recovery and 72.5% desalination from RO concentrate</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-4">Integrating RED into an RO–membrane distillation–RED system reduced electrical energy by 17% and specific energy (thermal and electrical) by 8% compared to RO alone</cite>. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Pre-desalinating seawater with reverse electrodialysis (RED) can decrease RO energy by producing energy and reducing seawater salinity, though area/capital costs are high unless assisted</cite>. In these configurations, ED/RED stages reduce the energy burden and/or volume sent to RO or to discharge, improving overall eco-efficiency.
- Ultra-pure water and demineralization: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Continuous electrodeionization (EDI) produces higher purity than ED or RO and requires low feed salt (<30 ppm); full-scale RO/CEDI plants produce ultra-pure water with conductivity <0.1 µS/cm</cite>. When feed can be pre-deionized to very low TDS, EDI coupled with RO achieves ultra-pure product with competitive energy performance compared to RO-only schemes. <cite id="907b5db6-3">CEDI is often combined with RO to reach purified or ultra-pure water grades</cite>.

When RO is more energy-efficient than ED/EDI
- High salinity (seawater to ~>5 g/L): <cite id="907b5db6-3">RO is more interesting for streams with concentrations higher than 5 g/L TDS</cite>. RO approaches near the osmotic limit and benefits from mature, high-flux membranes and low hydraulic pressure; representative specific energy is on the order of 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery for seawater RO. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO requires 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery, and pre-salting with RED can reduce this but adds area and cost</cite>. In such regimes, ED suffers from higher cell voltages across concentrated compartments and membrane polarization/ohmic drops, increasing energy per m³.
- Very low-permeate-purity targets with high-purity concentrate acceptable: RO’s solvent-shutoff can deliver permeate down to 0.1 µS/cm with appropriate pre/ post-treatment, whereas ED/EDI generally need lower feed salinity to reach the same purity, or hybridization with RO. <cite id="907b5db6-3">Continuous EDI requires feed <30 ppm to be effective, often leading to association with RO</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-3">RO/CEDI plants have produced ultra-pure water at conductivity <0.1 µS/cm</cite>. For deep desalination to ultra-pure product, RO alone or RO+EDI is often the practical choice.
- Temperature-limited ED conditions: ED energy scales with ionic strength and transport resistances; performance degrades at low salinity due to membrane hydrolysis and at high temperatures due to electrode kinetics, unless designed for thermal ED. <cite id="907b5db6-2">Hydrolysis and sediment formation are major problems for ED, causing clogging and requiring careful feed water control</cite>. In contrast, RO performance benefits from temperature increases in a way that is compatible with mature, robust systems.

Mechanisms: Why ED can be more efficient than RO at low salinity/high recovery
- Driving forces and transport: ED/EDI exploit electrical potential to drive ionic transport through ion-exchange membranes, avoiding the osmotic pressure-dominated solvent flux of RO. At low salinity, osmotic pressure differences are small, so ED can achieve high permeate recovery with lower voltage if stack resistance is controlled; ED’s direct control over salt removal by voltage allows recovery–quality trade-offs that RO cannot easily make without permeate fouling. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED can directly control salt removal by varying applied voltage</cite> and <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED is less sensitive to feed quality changes and offers higher water recovery at lower specific energy than RO</cite>.
- Ion specificity: ED/EDI remove ions via ion exchange, favoring divalent cations and targeted anions; RO treats all solute species equally as “osmotically active,” so energy depends primarily on total countercurrent pressure work. <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED generally removes high-charge salts well and is resistant to chloride and sediments; recovery can exceed 90%</cite>. This makes ED/EDI attractive for waters dominated by hardness and certain anions.
- Resistance and polarization: RO energy rises with required pressure to overcome osmotic pressure and hydraulic friction, while ED energy rises with cell voltage and ionic resistances (membranes/electrodes) and concentration polarization. ED benefits from higher recovery without tight salt rejection penalties when operated at low salinity; RO, by contrast, penalizes recovery due to increased osmotic pressure in the draw solution. <cite id="907b5db6-1">At 3 g/L, ED’s energy was lower than RO at 90% salt removal and 80% recovery; at 5 g/L, RO was lower</cite>.

Hybrid and real-world effluent contexts
- Industrial and stormwater de-icing salts: <cite id="907b5db6-1">For runoff loaded with road de-icing salts, ED offers higher recovery, is less sensitive to feed quality, and has lower specific energy; ED’s ability to control salt removal via voltage is advantageous</cite>. ED’s tolerance to chloride and sediment-laden waters and thin, robust membranes make it suitable, whereas RO requires extensive scaling and fouling control.
- Concentrate minimization and zero-liquid discharge: <cite id="907b5db6-4">ED can convert RO brine to potable water at 67.8% recovery and 72.5% desalination, reducing the volume of concentrated brine</cite>; RED integration can recover energy and lower overall specific energy compared to RO alone. <cite id="907b5db6-4">A hybrid RO–RED–membrane distillation system reduced electrical energy by 17% and specific energy by 8% versus RO</cite>. These designs improve total process eco-efficiency where RO brine is unavoidable.

Why studies disagree on which is “more energy-efficient”
- Metric definitions and reporting: <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO specific energy is often reported around 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery</cite>, while ED/EDI studies report energy per m³ of water or per unit salt removed. Bench studies often optimize ED voltage for target salt removal and report “lower” energy, whereas pilot/plant comparisons may reflect higher ED voltages and resistances at scale, or include pumps/heat. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED had lower energy at 3 g/L and 80% recovery for 90% salt removal, but required more energy than RO at 5 g/L for the same salt removal</cite>. Discrepancies arise when studies compare kWh/m³ of water versus kWh per unit salt removed, or when they evaluate different recovery/salt removal targets.
- Feed composition and chemistry assumptions: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED can control salt removal by adjusting voltage, which is especially useful when feed composition varies</cite>, but performance depends on ion valence, concentration, and presence of particulates and hardness. <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED is sensitive to hydrolysis and fouling; careful feedwater management is required</cite>. If a study assumes ideal, stable TDS without scaling/fouling, ED may look better than in practice; if it overestimates RO’s fouling or scaling penalties, RO may seem worse.
- Temperature and system design: <cite id="66a4642d-1">At low diluate concentrations (up to 0.1 M), RED/ED processes benefit from assisted operation to overcome high resistance, reducing area and increasing efficiency</cite>. If a study neglects stack/electrode resistances or concentration polarization, ED/EDI may be over-optimistic; conversely, if RO assumptions ignore temperature or brine handling, RO may be underestimated.
- Scale and configuration: <cite id="907b5db6-0">RO dominates installed capacity in brackish water desalination, reflecting maturity and cost curves</cite>, yet ED/EDI pilots can show advantages at specific salinity/recovery sweet spots. Hybrid configurations (e.g., NF–RO–ED) can change the energy balance by shifting divalent removal to ED to reduce scaling and allow recycle. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Assisted RED can make ED pre-treatment economically viable for lowering RO energy</cite> and <cite id="66a4642d-1">RED pre-treatment reduces RO energy by diluting and producing energy, but needs small applied potential to overcome resistance</cite>. Pilot-to-plant scaling, pre-treatment quality, and concentrate handling materially shift conclusions.
- Economic and environmental framing: <cite id="907b5db6-3">ED is generally better for <5 g/L TDS in cost effectiveness analyses</cite>, but studies may weight electricity price, carbon intensity, and infrastructure lifetime differently. Some works emphasize energy per m³, others include lifecycle emissions and energy of mixing, leading to different rankings. <cite id="907b5db6-4">Hybrid systems can reduce specific energy and electrical consumption, aiding eco-efficiency</cite>, which may not be captured uniformly across studies.

Practical decision guidance
- Use ED/EDI when: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Feed TDS is below ~5 g/L</cite>; <cite id="907b5db6-1">you need high recovery with controllable salt in the permeate</cite>; feed contains hardness and/or targeted monovalent anions; or you must minimize concentrate volume via ED of RO brine. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED’s voltage control over salt removal and higher tolerance to chloride/sediments</cite> make it attractive for de-icing runoff and similar streams. <cite id="907b5db6-4">ED can recover substantial water from RO brine</cite>.
- Use RO when: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Feed TDS exceeds ~5 g/L (especially seawater)</cite>; you need very high-purity permeate without extensive pre-deionization; or you have mature infrastructure and can manage brine. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO typically needs 2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery</cite>, and hybrid pre-treatment can reduce this, but RO’s solvent-shutoff limits complicate very high-recovery, low-salinity targets without additional energy.
- For ultra-pure water: <cite id="907b5db6-3">Combine RO with EDI to leverage RO’s solvent rejection and EDI’s continuous ion removal at low TDS</cite>, as demonstrated by full-scale RO/CEDI plants producing <0.1 µS/cm water. <cite id="907b5db6-3">CEDI is often associated with RO for purified/ultra-pure water</cite>.
- For industrial effluents: <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED is viable for road-deicing runoff with high chloride and suspended solids, offering higher recovery and lower specific energy than RO</cite>; however, <cite id="907b5db6-2">design must mitigate hydrolysis/fouling risks</cite>.
- For brine minimization: <cite id="907b5db6-4">ED or RED stages can convert RO concentrate to potable water or energy, reducing brine volume and specific energy compared to RO alone</cite>.

Key quantitative anchors
- <cite id="907b5db6-1">At 3 g/L salinity, ED used less energy than RO to achieve 90% salt removal and 80% water recovery; at 5 g/L, RO was more energy-efficient for similar salt removal</cite>. <cite id="907b5db6-3">A practical rule-of-thumb is ED favored for <5 g/L TDS and RO for >5 g/L TDS in cost-energy terms</cite>.
- <cite id="66a4642d-1">Seawater RO typically requires ~2–3 kWh/m³ at 50% recovery; ED/RED pre-treatment can reduce this but increases membrane area unless assisted</cite>. <cite id="66a4642d-1">Assisted RED (small applied potential) reduces diluate resistance, enabling more efficient ED-RO hybridization</cite>.
- <cite id="907b5db6-2">Reported ED power consumption spans about 1.2–2.5 kWh/m³ in some field/pilot implementations, with potential to remove 1 kg salt per <1 kWh under optimized lab conditions, though fouling and electro-osmosis can degrade performance</cite>.
- <cite id="907b5db6-2">ED recovery often exceeds 90% and can be economical for balanced TDS, while RO faces fouling/hydraulic penalties and brine volume constraints</cite>.

Bottom line
ED/EDI are generally more energy-efficient than RO for low-TDS waters with acceptable ion selectivity, when high recovery is desired, and in hybrid schemes that pre-deplete ions or treat RO brines; RO is typically more efficient at higher salinity and for very deep desalination to ultra-pure product without extensive pre-deionization. <cite id="907b5db6-1">ED’s advantage at low salinity and controllable salt removal</cite>, <cite id="907b5db6-3">its better recovery and cost-effectiveness below ~5 g/L TDS</cite>, and <cite id="907b5db6-4">its ability to recover from RO concentrate</cite> explain many comparative findings. Studies disagree because they differ in metrics (kWh/m³ vs per-salt basis), scales (bench/pilot/plant), water chemistry assumptions, resistance models and polarization effects, pre-treatment quality, and whether hybridization is allowed, among other factors. <cite id="907b5db6-1">Where ED is operated at low salinity with tuned voltage and minimal fouling</cite> and <cite id="66a4642d-1">where ED pre-treatment is engineered to overcome low-diluate resistance (e.g., assisted RED)</cite>, ED/EDI often appear more energy-efficient; at higher salinity or for the deepest demineralization without hybridization, RO typically wins on energy per m³. </answer>

Title: Runoff water loaded with road de‐icing salts: Occurrence, environmental impact and treatment processes

Title: Hybrid renewable energy systems for desalination
Snippet: Today, all commercial electrodialysis machines are from EDR type. By preventing the accumulation of ions on the surface of the membranes in the reverse electrodialysis method, these types of devices can dehydrate at higher capacities (Voutchkov 2012). 

The energy required for this method is directly proportional to the amount of water salinity. Generally, this method can remove the appropriate form of high-charge particles such as monatomic and polyatomic salts, silicates, nitrates and radium, but these devices can be used to absorb low-charge particles such as organic matter and organisms such as bacteria. The following table presents a comparison of particle outflow efficiencies in the recovering process by ED and RO methods. The important issue to notice from this table is that ED extracts fewer amounts of useful minerals for humans and this makes the desalination process more attractive than reverse osmosis or thermal distillation (Table 4). 

Hydrolysis and sediment formation are two major problems for this method. Consequently, the membrane used in this method is subjected to clogging deposition, so some precaution actions must be applied to the inlet water. The rate of recovery with this method is over 90% and is very economical to set up and use for balanced TDS. However, ED and EDR membranes are highly resistant to acidic and alkali environments. This process is more resistant to chloride and sediments (compared with RO) and is significantly thinner than RO membranes (Micale et al. 2009).

Title: Electrodialytic Processes: Market Overview, Membrane Phenomena, Recent Developments and Sustainable Strategies
Snippet: Desalination of sea water using conventional ED is a robust process with moderate energy requirement. ED represents 4% of the desalination capacity worldwide, while reverse osmosis (RO) stands for 64% and thermal distillation processes for about 30%. In addition to a more efficient energy use than for thermal processes, ED has several advantages compared to RO. Lighter pre-and post-treatments lead to longer membrane lifespan, while higher temperature tolerance and selectivity allow more flexibility. ED has also better water recovery [6,285]. In terms of cost effectiveness, ED is generally better for water with less than 5 g of total dissolved solids (TDS) per liter, while RO is more interesting for streams with concentrations higher than 5 g TDS/L [192]. Due to this complementarity and in order to reach deeper desalinations by maintaining the eco-efficiency of the process, researchers are studying the coupling of electrodialytic technologies with other operation units such as pressure-driven membrane filtration.

Continuous electrodeionization leads to higher water purity than ED or RO due its enhanced conductivity (c.f. Section 4.8), however it requires less concentrated water as the feed stream (<30 ppm). Therefore, a viable strategy is to associate CEDI with RO, ED or both [205]. Ho and Wood [286] evaluated the performances of a full-scale RO/CEDI plant for deionized water production. After 18 months, 3.4 million m 3 of ultra-pure water (conductivity < 0.1 µS/cm i.e., resistivity > 10 Ω.cm) was produced. More recently, a high efficiency reverse osmosis (HERO™)/FEDI ® process has been implemented in Egypt as a water purification strategy [210]. Nile water and various effluents were successfully converted in ultra-pure water with resistivity ranging between 10 and18 MΩ.cm. Water discharged by geothermal plants is gaining more and more interest as a sustainable source for fresh water [206,287] so current strategies involve RO applied geothermal water followed by CEDI. Although such processes were originally aiming for ultra-pure water (0.05-0.10 µS/cm), recent implementations only manage to reach purified water grade

Title: Electrodialysis Processes an Answer to Industrial Sustainability: Toward the Concept of Eco-Circular Economy?—A Review
Snippet: Seawater reverse osmosis (RO) is the main technology used for the desalination of seawater. Despite global attention, several RO limits remain, such as final water quality, recovery factor, cost, and brine disposal [93], which are major issues. Indeed, the recovery factor is limited to 50% by the osmotic phenomenon [94]. Hence, a large volume of brine is produced and has negative impacts on the environment, such as damage to water ecosystems. In this context, reverse electrodialysis (RED), conventional electrodialysis, and electrodialysis metathesis (EDM) were proposed as answers to improve seawater RO processes. 

Reverse electrodialysis (RED) showed an interesting capacity when integrated into an RO-membrane distillation-RED desalination system [95]. This membrane process is based on a conventional ED configuration, stacking CEMs and AEMs. Unlike in ED, the driving force comes from the ion's potential differences between "High Concentration" and "Low Concentration" compartments, which creates an electricity gradient instead of applying an external potential difference. RED is known for its renewable energy generation through the flux of ions that reaches electrodes where redox reactions allow the continuous generation of electricity [95]. The most optimized hybrid system demonstrated an improvement in the energy efficiency of the global process, with up to 17% reduction in electrical energy consumption and 8% in specific energy consumption (thermal and electrical energy per volume of desalted water) compared to RO alone [94]. The study demonstrated a new step forward in the implementation of zero-liquid discharge systems and low-energy desalination thanks to the ability to produce renewable energy and drinkable water [94]. No EE score was determined through the study to compare both methods. 

Conventional ED also demonstrated the capacity to treat concentrated brine obtained after desalination by RO [96]. ED allowed the production, from RO brine, of fresh water with a water recovery rate of 67.8% and a desalination rate of 72.5%.

Today, all commercial electrodialysis machines are from EDR type. By preventing the accumulation of ions on the surface of the membranes in the reverse electrodialysis method, these types of devices can dehydrate at higher capacities (Voutchkov 2012). 

The energy required for this method is directly proportional to the amount of water salinity. Generally, this method can remove the appropriate form of high-charge particles such as monatomic and polyatomic salts, silicates, nitrates and radium, but these devices can be used to absorb low-charge particles such as organic matter and organisms such as bacteria. The following table presents a comparison of particle outflow efficiencies in the recovering process by ED and RO methods. The important issue to notice from this table is that ED extracts fewer amounts of useful minerals for humans and this makes the desalination process more attractive than reverse osmosis or thermal distillation (Table 4). 

Hydrolysis and sediment formation are two major problems for this method. Consequently, the membrane used in this method is subjected to clogging deposition, so some precaution actions must be applied to the inlet water. The rate of recovery with this method is over 90% and is very economical to set up and use for balanced TDS. However, ED and EDR membranes are highly resistant to acidic and alkali environments. This process is more resistant to chloride and sediments (compared with RO) and is significantly thinner than RO membranes (Micale et al. 2009).

snippet.text:
Desalination of sea water using conventional ED is a robust process with moderate energy requirement. ED represents 4% of the desalination capacity worldwide, while reverse osmosis (RO) stands for 64% and thermal distillation processes for about 30%. In addition to a more efficient energy use than for thermal processes, ED has several advantages compared to RO. Lighter pre-and post-treatments lead to longer membrane lifespan, while higher temperature tolerance and selectivity allow more flexibility. ED has also better water recovery [6,285]. In terms of cost effectiveness, ED is generally better for water with less than 5 g of total dissolved solids (TDS) per liter, while RO is more interesting for streams with concentrations higher than 5 g TDS/L [192]. Due to this complementarity and in order to reach deeper desalinations by maintaining the eco-efficiency of the process, researchers are studying the coupling of electrodialytic technologies with other operation units such as pressure-driven membrane filtration.

Continuous electrodeionization leads to higher water purity than ED or RO due its enhanced conductivity (c.f. Section 4.8), however it requires less concentrated water as the feed stream (<30 ppm). Therefore, a viable strategy is to associate CEDI with RO, ED or both [205]. Ho and Wood [286] evaluated the performances of a full-scale RO/CEDI plant for deionized water production. After 18 months, 3.4 million m 3 of ultra-pure water (conductivity < 0.1 µS/cm i.e., resistivity > 10 Ω.cm) was produced. More recently, a high efficiency reverse osmosis (HERO™)/FEDI ® process has been implemented in Egypt as a water purification strategy [210]. Nile water and various effluents were successfully converted in ultra-pure water with resistivity ranging between 10 and18 MΩ.cm. Water discharged by geothermal plants is gaining more and more interest as a sustainable source for fresh water [206,287] so current strategies involve RO applied geothermal water followed by CEDI. Although such processes were originally aiming for ultra-pure water (0.05-0.10 µS/cm), recent implementations only manage to reach purified water grade

snippet.text:
Seawater reverse osmosis (RO) is the main technology used for the desalination of seawater. Despite global attention, several RO limits remain, such as final water quality, recovery factor, cost, and brine disposal [93], which are major issues. Indeed, the recovery factor is limited to 50% by the osmotic phenomenon [94]. Hence, a large volume of brine is produced and has negative impacts on the environment, such as damage to water ecosystems. In this context, reverse electrodialysis (RED), conventional electrodialysis, and electrodialysis metathesis (EDM) were proposed as answers to improve seawater RO processes. 

Reverse electrodialysis (RED) showed an interesting capacity when integrated into an RO-membrane distillation-RED desalination system [95]. This membrane process is based on a conventional ED configuration, stacking CEMs and AEMs. Unlike in ED, the driving force comes from the ion's potential differences between "High Concentration" and "Low Concentration" compartments, which creates an electricity gradient instead of applying an external potential difference. RED is known for its renewable energy generation through the flux of ions that reaches electrodes where redox reactions allow the continuous generation of electricity [95]. The most optimized hybrid system demonstrated an improvement in the energy efficiency of the global process, with up to 17% reduction in electrical energy consumption and 8% in specific energy consumption (thermal and electrical energy per volume of desalted water) compared to RO alone [94]. The study demonstrated a new step forward in the implementation of zero-liquid discharge systems and low-energy desalination thanks to the ability to produce renewable energy and drinkable water [94]. No EE score was determined through the study to compare both methods. 

Conventional ED also demonstrated the capacity to treat concentrated brine obtained after desalination by RO [96]. ED allowed the production, from RO brine, of fresh water with a water recovery rate of 67.8% and a desalination rate of 72.5%.

Title: Capacitive deionisation for water desalination review: experimental and simulation
Snippet: While RO is effective for high salinity waters, CDI requires less specific energy demand associated with RO systems, making it more suitable for lower salinity waters. Unlike electrodialysis, which uses ion exchange membranes and can handle a broader range of salinities, CDI is more restricted but offers simpler operations and lower energy costs. 

Furthermore, the recent advances in hybrid CDI technologies such as RO-CDI [59], NF-CDI [60] and RO-MCDI-RED [61] show promise in addressing some of the inherent limitations of CDI, particularly in terms of scalability and operational efficiency [9]. Maheshwari et al. demonstrated that combining nanofiltration and CDI can effectively treat RO retentate while maintaining low energy consumption (~3.5 kWh/m 3 ), making it suitable for high-performance wastewater treatment [60]. 

In a recent study, Lim et al. [62] quantitatively compared the performance of flow-electrode capacitive deionization (FCDI) with brackish water reverse osmosis (BWRO) and seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO). Their validated simulation model demonstrated that under low salinity conditions, FCDI could achieve a specific energy consumption (SEC) as low as 2.7% of BWRO's SEC. Moreover, the study showed that with appropriate membrane area scaling and system optimization, FCDI can remain competitive even in higher salinity applications, offering a viable low-energy alternative to conventional membrane-based desalination technologies.

Title: Development of Hybrid Membrane Systems for Highly Mineralized Waste Utilization in the Power Industry
Snippet: Comparing electrodialysis systems operating in stand-alone and hybrid configurations, it can be concluded that the cost of desalination of the electrodialysis product is always higher for a stand-alone system since the degree of product purification is completely dependent on the operation of the electrodialyzer. Study [30] compared various configurations of membrane systems for desalination and concentration of effluents: a standard single-stage reverse osmosis (RO) system, a hybrid reverse osmosis-electrodialysis (RO-ED) system, a nanofiltration-reverse osmosis (NF-RO) system, and a nanofiltration-reverse osmosis-electrodialysis (NF-RO-ED) system. Indicators such as the percentage of diluate and concentrate yield, the total salt content of the concentrate (TSC), the energy expended, the risk of scale formation, and the possibility of reusing products were evaluated (Table 1). The most effective was the NF-RO-ED system, which is capable of producing a highly concentrated brine close to saturation with respect to sodium chloride and the largest volume of diluate. The brine can be further used in the production of table salt or in the chlorine industry. In the case of one-stage RO, for every 1 m 3 of demineralized water, 0.574 m 3 of concentrate (OSC 60 g/L) is produced, which must be disposed of, which creates additional costs. The integration of NF and RO does not significantly change the salinity and volume of the resulting brine compared to the RO configuration. The introduction of ED helps to solve the problem of a large volume of low-mineralized waste. The NF-RO-ED system produces less clean water than the RO-ED configuration but produces a more concentrated brine. In the NF-RO-ED system, NF removes most of the divalent hardness ions from the RO-ED circuit. Due to the reduced risk of scale formation in the ED module, recirculation occurs on the concentrate side, resulting in a concentrate that is practically saturated with sodium chloride [31].

Reverse electrodialysis (RED) showed an interesting capacity when integrated into an RO-membrane distillation-RED desalination system [95]. This membrane process is based on a conventional ED configuration, stacking CEMs and AEMs. Unlike in ED, the driving force comes from the ion's potential differences between "High Concentration" and "Low Concentration" compartments, which creates an electricity gradient instead of applying an external potential difference. RED is known for its renewable energy generation through the flux of ions that reaches electrodes where redox reactions allow the continuous generation of electricity [95]. The most optimized hybrid system demonstrated an improvement in the energy efficiency of the global process, with up to 17% reduction in electrical energy consumption and 8% in specific energy consumption (thermal and electrical energy per volume of desalted water) compared to RO alone [94]. The study demonstrated a new step forward in the implementation of zero-liquid discharge systems and low-energy desalination thanks to the ability to produce renewable energy and drinkable water [94]. No EE score was determined through the study to compare both methods. 

Conventional ED also demonstrated the capacity to treat concentrated brine obtained after desalination by RO [96]. ED allowed the production, from RO brine, of fresh water with a water recovery rate of 67.8% and a desalination rate of 72.5%.

documents.snippet: Comparing electrodialysis systems operating in stand-alone and hybrid configurations, it can be concluded that the cost of desalination of the electrodialysis product is always higher for a stand-alone system since the degree of product purification is completely dependent on the operation of the electrodialyzer. Study [30] compared various configurations of membrane systems for desalination and concentration of effluents: a standard single-stage reverse osmosis (RO) system, a hybrid reverse osmosis-electrodialysis (RO-ED) system, a nanofiltration-reverse osmosis (NF-RO) system, and a nanofiltration-reverse osmosis-electrodialysis (NF-RO-ED) system. Indicators such as the percentage of diluate and concentrate yield, the total salt content of the concentrate (TSC), the energy expended, the risk of scale formation, and the possibility of reusing products were evaluated (Table 1). The most effective was the NF-RO-ED system, which is capable of producing a highly concentrated brine close to saturation with respect to sodium chloride and the largest volume of diluate. The brine can be further used in the production of table salt or in the chlorine industry. In the case of one-stage RO, for every 1 m 3 of demineralized water, 0.574 m 3 of concentrate (OSC 60 g/L) is produced, which must be disposed of, which creates additional costs. The integration of NF and RO does not significantly change the salinity and volume of the resulting brine compared to the RO configuration. The introduction of ED helps to solve the problem of a large volume of low-mineralized waste. The NF-RO-ED system produces less clean water than the RO-ED configuration but produces a more concentrated brine. In the NF-RO-ED system, NF removes most of the divalent hardness ions from the RO-ED circuit. Due to the reduced risk of scale formation in the ED module, recirculation occurs on the concentrate side, resulting in a concentrate that is practically saturated with sodium chloride [31].

Title: Assisted reverse electrodialysis—principles, mechanisms, and potential
Snippet: Although seawater reverse osmosis (RO) is nearing its thermodynamic minimum energy limit, it is still an energy-intensive process, requiring 2–3 kWh/m³ at a recovery of 50%. Pre-desalination of the seawater by reverse electrodialysis (RED), using an impaired water source, can further decrease this energy demand by producing energy and reducing the seawater concentration. However, RED is hampered by the initial high resistance of the fresh water source, resulting in a high required membrane area (i.e., high investment costs). In this paper, a new process is presented that can overcome this initial resistance and decrease the RED investment cost without the need for additional infrastructure: assisted RED (ARED). In ARED, a small potential difference is applied in the direction of the natural salinity gradient, increasing the ionic transport rate and rapidly decreasing the initial diluate resistance. This decreasing resistance is shown to outweigh any negative effects caused by, for example, concentration polarization, resulting in a process that is more efficient than theoretically expected. As this effect is mainly important at low diluate concentrations (up to 0.1 M), ARED is proposed as a first step in an economic and energy efficient (A)RED-RO hybrid process.Seawater desalination: assisting reverse osmosisCoupling reverse osmosis with assisted reverse electrodialysis can reduce the cost of seawater desalination. While reverse osmosis currently accounts for more than 60% of our worldwide seawater desalination capacity, this crucial process operates at a high energy demand. A reverse electrodialysis (RED) pre-treatment of seawater, diluted with a waste water stream, reduces the energy demand by producing energy and by reducing the concentration of the seawater subjected to reverse osmosis. Nonetheless, low transport rates in RED require high-membrane surface areas, making the costs impractical. A team led by Marjolein Vanoppen at Gent University in Belgium design an assisted RED pre-treatment process, where a small potential difference is applied in the direction of the salinity gradient, increasing the ionic transport rate and decreasing the required membrane surface area, thus offering a more economically viable alternative.

Moreover, the ultrafiltration treatment process was observed with an average cake thickness of 0.043 m over six months; equivalent to 2.4 × 10 −4 m per day. Also, 0.016 m six month of cake thickness was observed from the reverse osmosis; equivalent to 8.9 × 10 −5 m per day.

Snippet: Electrodialysis is a relatively high efficiency of desalination technology in parallel with Reverse Osmosis technology (RO). However, there are some disadvantages compared to RO technology, so it is not widely to use. Nguyen Hoai Chau et al. (2005) [35] have applied this technology to remove salinity, hardness and suspended solid in ground water with the experimental model scale of 100 l/h capacitys. The research has compared the performance of three different membranes: Vietnamese membrane made from cellulose acetate; Russian membranes and US membranes. The cylindrical membrane is 200 mm of diameter and 12.56 cm 2 area of each. The working electrode is made of Titanium covered an anti-corrosive layer. The results showed that three membranes had similar performance that reached as 83%, 66%, 65% performance for hardness, suspended solid, desalination removal efficiencies respectively. This study demonstrates that electrolysis technology has potential in field of desalination with low power consumption, not over 1 kWh per 1 kg salt to be removed. However, this method still has some limitations that affect the performance by osmosis and electro-osmosis process, the fouling membranes by presence of organic and inorganic substances. 

In addition to desalination, the electrodialysis is also investigated for the treatment of nitrogen compounds in groundwater. Model of 30-60 l/h capacity included titanium electrodes covered by noble metal oxide layer for anti-corrosive, 53 VDC of voltage, a range of 0.75-1.5A current density. The results illustrated over 99% ammonium removal efficiency when input ammonium concentration was 10.4 mg/l. The nitrite and nitrate removal efficiency were 80% and 60%, respectively. The power consumption for this process ranged from 1.2 to 2.5 kWh/m 3 (Nguyen Thu Tra, 2005 [36]).

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer clearly demonstrates that its own cited sources contain conflicting findings about ED vs RO energy efficiency. It explicitly states that at 3 g/L TDS, ED had lower energy consumption than RO at 90% salt removal and 80% recovery, while at 5 g/L ED required more energy than RO under similar conditions (cite 907b5db6-1). It also cites opposing verdicts: some sources show ED is more efficient for <5 g/L TDS (cite 907b5db6-3), while others favor RO for >5 g/L TDS. The answer attributes these conflicts to concrete boundary conditions including: (1) feedwater salinity range (the 3-5 g/L TDS threshold), (2) water recovery rates (ED achieving >90% vs RO's lower recovery), (3) salt removal targets (90% vs other levels), and (4) hybrid configurations. The section 'Why studies disagree' explicitly lists metric definitions, feed composition, temperature, scale, and economic framing as sources of disagreement. The answer does not issue a single uniform verdict but instead presents a nuanced view acknowledging when each technology is favored.
other_issues: The answer conflates electrodialysis (ED) with electrodeionization (EDI) in places where they are distinct technologies with different mechanisms and applications. EDI is typically used for ultra-pure water production from already-low-TDS feeds, while ED is for general desalination.

Some citations appear to be used for claims they may not directly support. For example, cite 907b5db6-2 is cited for very specific power consumption numbers (1.2-2.5 kWh/m³, <1 kWh per kg salt) without clear verification these exact figures appear in that source.
The answer includes reverse electrodialysis (RED) extensively, which is an energy-generating technology rather than a desalination method, potentially muddying the core ED vs RO comparison.
Minor organizational issue: the 'Why studies disagree' section appears midway through rather than being clearly signposted as the main reconciliation of conflicting evidence.
The quantitative anchor claiming '1 kg salt per <1 kWh under optimized lab conditions' for ED seems suspiciously efficient and may be a misinterpretation or hallucination without clearer sourcing.

However, it has notable issues with conflating ED/EDI/RED technologies, potentially unsupported quantitative claims, and organizational clarity. Despite these problems, the core task of showing and explaining conflicting evidence is accomplished.
